member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.ContactCount.Four
member.summary: Creates four spline-following contacts arranged as a rectangle around the configured anchor.

remarks.para: Value 4. A spline is a curved path. The anchor is the connection position relative to the main body. Its anchor frame is the set of directions built from the configured axis and secondary axis, so it turns with the body. The rectangle uses both dimensions of the configured size: size.y sets front/back spacing and size.x sets side-to-side spacing. Each direction is offset by half its configured spacing in the anchor frame before conversion from the body’s local space. A zero spacing collapses the matching separation rather than being replaced with an automatic size. The spacings use Unity distance units; one unit represents one meter when the scene uses that convention. Initial contact creation rotates and translates these offsets with the body without multiplying them by its Transform scale.

The solver calculates front/back path targets, then offsets a pair to each side using the side-to-side spacing. Each target controls a Contact physics body connected to the main body by a joint, a physics connection that limits how two bodies move. The individual contacts are constructed with free angular motion; their spread target positions still constrain the main body’s motion and orientation. Four does not mean four collision points reported by Unity. Later front/back query positions are transformed from the body's local coordinates using TransformPoint, which includes its scale. The side-to-side target offset instead uses half of size.x directly after world rotation, without body scale. Resizing the body therefore does not uniformly rescale initial contact placement and all later target spacing.

Configure this before SplineJoint.Awake, Unity’s initialization callback, creates the contacts. A callback is a routine called to perform or report an action. Changing the enum after initialization does not rebuild the contact list, and the four-contact solver expects entries for all four contacts.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.ContactCount.One
member.summary: Creates one spline-following physics contact at the body’s configured anchor.

remarks.para: Value 1. A spline is a curved path. The anchor is the connection position relative to the main body, and a Rigidbody is a body simulated by Unity's physics system. The SplineJoint builds one Contact from its anchor position and anchor orientation. A Contact creates a controlled physics body and a joint connecting it to the main Rigidbody; the solver moves its target toward the configured path. A joint constrains how connected physics bodies may move.

This contact receives the SplineJoint’s configured twist, swing and sideways-motion settings directly. Twist turns around the configured axis; swing tilts away from it. The one-point solver samples the path nearest the body’s anchor and also requests a rotational spring correction: a restoring adjustment toward a chosen orientation through the joint's target rotation. That correction is skipped if twist is locked, both swing directions are locked, or either swing angle limit is greater than 90 degrees. This is a constraint setup, not a count of collision events or hands gripping an object.

Choose the count before SplineJoint.Awake, Unity’s initialization callback, builds its contact list. A callback is a routine called to perform or report an action. Changing the enum afterward does not automatically rebuild that list.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.ContactCount.Two
member.summary: Creates two spline-following contacts on opposite sides of the configured anchor.

remarks.para: Value 2. A spline is a curved path. The anchor is the connection position relative to the main body. Its anchor frame supplies directions built from the configured axis and secondary axis; these directions turn with the body. The two anchor positions are a front/back pair in the configured anchor frame. Their offsets use half of size.y, the configured front/back spacing, on each side of the anchor before conversion from the body’s local space. For example, size.y = 1 creates contacts roughly 0.5 Unity distance units on either side along the anchor directions; half the spacing is used for each offset. One distance unit represents one meter when the scene uses that convention. Initial placement rotates and translates the offsets with the body without multiplying them by its Transform scale. Later Solve and PlaceOnSpline queries use TransformPoint, which does include body scale when converting local query positions to the world. Resizing the body therefore does not uniformly rescale contact setup and later path queries, and this example does not promise an exact contact-body separation on every frame.

The solver calculates two target points along the path and updates the corresponding Contact constraints. Each Contact creates a controlled physics body connected to the main body by a joint, which constrains their relative movement. The individual contacts are constructed with free angular motion; the separated contact targets still influence the main body’s orientation.

These contacts are created during SplineJoint.Awake, Unity’s initialization callback—a routine called to prepare the component. Switching from One to Two later does not allocate the missing contact merely because the enum changed.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.DampenContactDrive.maximumForce
member.summary: Caps the force from each contact joint's linear X drive when these settings are applied.

remarks.para: A joint is a simulated connection between two bodies. Its drive acts like a motor that pushes them toward a chosen relative speed along the joint’s X direction. The cap is in newtons. SplineJoint copies this value to each Contact's ConfigurableJoint.xDrive.maximumForce. It limits the drive along that joint's X axis, not the total collision force on the object or the sum over every contact.

positionDamper is the damping coefficient, in newton-seconds per meter. It multiplies the difference between the configured target speed and current relative speed along the joint's X direction, with both speeds in meters per second. Current relative speed means how fast the connected bodies move past each other along that axis. A larger coefficient can request more force, but this cap still limits the drive. A cap of zero permits no force from that drive.

Changing a separate DampenContactDrive value does not automatically update existing joints. The owning SplineJoint must apply its configuration, or SplineJoint.SetLinearXDriveMaxForce can apply a supplied cap to existing contacts. That live setter does not save the supplied cap back into this stored settings pair.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.DampenContactDrive.positionDamper
member.summary: Controls how strongly a contact's linear X drive resists a difference from its target speed.

remarks.para: A joint is a simulated connection between two bodies. Its drive acts like a motor that pushes them toward a chosen relative speed along the joint’s X direction. The coefficient is newton-seconds per meter: multiplying it by a speed difference in meters per second gives a force term in newtons. The speed difference is between the drive's configured target speed and the bodies' current relative speed along the joint's X axis, meaning how fast the connected bodies move past each other along that axis. At a target speed of zero, this damper resists that relative motion; a nonzero target can make it act like a speed-following motor.

For an illustrative coefficient of 100 N·s/m and speed difference of 0.5 m/s, the damping term requests 50 N before maximumForce limits the drive. With a 20 N cap, increasing the damper further does not lift that cap. These are example force terms, not a promise about the measured motion under all physics constraints.

SplineJoint copies this field into each Contact's ConfigurableJoint.xDrive.positionDamper. The coefficient is not seconds of smoothing or a spring that pulls toward a target position. Changing a detached copy of this struct does not update a live joint.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.Handedness.BOTH
member.summary: Selects both hand sides for an operation that supports a two-hand selection.

remarks.para: Its numeric value is 3. PhysicsRig.ResetHands accepts it and processes the right hand before the left in each phase. ResetHands starts a new selection only when no hand reset is already running. A call during an existing reset is ignored: it does not replace that reset’s selection or queue another reset. It is a selection for that operation, not proof that both hands are grabbing an object simultaneously.

The checked reset routine detaches the selected hands, waits for a physics-update step, disables collision detection before resetting each selected physical hand, then waits using a configured 0.1 seconds of scaled game time before enabling collisions again. Scaled game time follows the game-speed multiplier: 1 is normal speed, 0.5 is half speed and 0 pauses that clock. The coroutine resumes on a later frame after the wait, so this is a configured delay rather than a promise of exactly 0.1 elapsed seconds. It runs as a coroutine, a sequence that can pause and continue over several frames.

A rig is the group of objects representing the player’s body and controls; a skeleton hand is the hand-bone representation, separate from its controller and its physical collision hand. ControllerRig.GetController and GameWorldSkeletonRig.GetSkeletonHand each return one object, so they return null for BOTH. Query LEFT and RIGHT separately when you need both controller or skeleton references.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.Handedness.LEFT
member.summary: Selects the rig's left-hand controller, skeleton hand or left-side reset operation.

remarks.para: Its numeric value is 1. A rig is the group of objects representing the player’s body and controls; a skeleton hand is the hand-bone representation, separate from its controller and its physical collision hand. ControllerRig.GetController returns leftController for this selection; GameWorldSkeletonRig.GetSkeletonHand returns its left skeleton reference. Those lookups do not grab or move the hand, and the stored reference can still be null if the rig is not ready.

PhysicsRig.ResetHands with LEFT runs its reset sequence for the left side only when it can start a new reset. ResetHands starts a new selection only when no hand reset is already running. A call during an existing reset is ignored: it does not replace that reset’s selection or queue another reset. These are the rig's left/right sides, not a choice of which physical controller is the user's dominant hand.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.Handedness.RIGHT

remarks.para: Its numeric value is 2. A rig is the group of objects representing the player’s body and controls; a skeleton hand is the hand-bone representation, separate from its controller and its physical collision hand. ControllerRig.GetController returns rightController for this selection; GameWorldSkeletonRig.GetSkeletonHand returns its right skeleton reference. These lookups select an existing reference; they do not attach, grab or reset the hand themselves.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.Handedness.UNDEFINED
member.summary: Selects neither side in the checked hand lookups and reset routine.

remarks.para: Its numeric value is 0. ControllerRig.GetController and GameWorldSkeletonRig.GetSkeletonHand return null for it. It does not mean either available hand or both hands.

PhysicsRig.ResetHands does not detach or reset either side for this value, although its coroutine can still run the waiting/cleanup stages. A coroutine is a sequence that pauses and continues over frames. Pass LEFT, RIGHT or BOTH for an actual hand reset.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.HibernationBodyInfo.angularVelocity
member.summary: Saved rotation rate used when restoring a body that was awake before hibernation.

remarks.para: This is a rotation-rate vector in radians per second: its direction gives the rotation axis and its magnitude gives the spin speed. It is not an orientation or a set of Euler angles.

CopyFrom updates it only for a body that is not sleeping. CopyTo applies it and wakes the body only when the saved isSleeping flag is false. A sleeping-body capture leaves this vector unchanged, so old rotation rates can remain in the snapshot.
Editing it changes a later awake-state restoration, rather than immediately rotating the live body. The restored constraints can still restrict rotation.

The components use the scene’s world axes. One full turn is about 6.28 radians, so (0, 6.28, 0) represents roughly one turn per second about world Y before any restored rotation locks. This is an illustrative conversion, not a promised unrestricted rotation.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.HibernationBodyInfo.constraints
member.summary: Saved movement and rotation locks reapplied when the body leaves hibernation.

remarks.para: These are flags that can be combined, such as FreezePositionY to block vertical movement, or FreezeAll to block every movement and rotation axis. Position locks use scene world axes; rotation locks use the body's inertia frame, the axes that describe its resistance to turning.

CopyFrom saves the live Rigidbody constraints and CopyTo writes them back. MarrowBody temporarily uses FreezeAll during hibernation. Editing this snapshot changes the locks restored later, not the live body's current constraints.
A Rigidbody is the component that represents an object’s movement and rotation in the physics simulation.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.HibernationBodyInfo.inertiaTensor
member.summary: Saved resistance to changes in the body's rotation, initially reapplied by CopyTo.

remarks.para: The three components describe resistance about the body's inertia axes through its center of mass, the body’s balance point. Those axes are oriented by the Rigidbody's inertiaTensorRotation. A larger component requires more turning force to produce the same change in rotation speed about that axis.

CopyFrom captures the live inertiaTensor and CopyTo sets it again, whether the saved body was sleeping or awake. This snapshot does not store inertiaTensorRotation, so it does not also restore the orientation of those axes.

MarrowBody's normal unhibernate path calls INTResetMass after CopyTo. It follows any Host links to the root body, then recalculates that root body's inertia when it is active in the scene, not marked as hibernating, and has a Rigidbody. If this snapshot belongs to that root body, an edited inertia value can therefore be replaced during the full restoration path.

A Rigidbody is the component that represents an object’s movement and rotation in the physics simulation. These inertia values use mass times distance squared, normally kilogram·metre². With the same turning force and an unlocked axis, doubling a positive component halves the rate at which rotation speed changes about that axis; the later root-body recalculation can still replace this edited cache as described above.
Each Host link points to another MarrowBody; the root is the last body in that chain, with no further Host.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.HibernationBodyInfo.isSleeping
member.summary: Records whether the body was sleeping when this snapshot was captured.

remarks.para: Sleeping means a body at rest is left out of active physics motion calculations until it wakes. This is saved state, rather than a live query of the current body.

CopyFrom records IsSleeping. With this flag true, CopyTo calls Sleep and does not apply the saved velocity vectors. With false, it restores both velocities and calls WakeUp. The other saved settings are restored in both cases.
CopyFrom does not refresh the velocity vectors when capturing a sleeping body. Changing this flag to false afterward can make restoration use older stored velocities.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.HibernationBodyInfo.sleepThreshold
member.summary: Saved energy-per-mass threshold used for deciding when the restored body can go to sleep.

remarks.para: The threshold compares motion energy divided by body mass, rather than total energy alone. A larger value permits sleeping at a higher amount of motion energy per mass; this is not a timer or a speed value.

CopyFrom captures Rigidbody.sleepThreshold and CopyTo restores it in both the sleeping and awake branches. MarrowBody temporarily sets the live threshold to positive infinity while hibernating, then restores this saved value.
Changing the cache affects later restoration. The saved isSleeping flag separately decides whether CopyTo calls Sleep or WakeUp immediately.

A Rigidbody is the component that represents an object’s movement and rotation in the physics simulation. Sleeping temporarily pauses the body’s active motion calculations. Motion energy is the energy in moving and spinning. This threshold uses energy per kilogram, normally joules per kilogram (equivalent to metre²/second²). For illustration, 0.02 joules of motion energy divided by 2 kilograms gives 0.01 joules per kilogram; this arithmetic does not predict an exact sleep time or a single speed at which every body sleeps.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.HibernationBodyInfo.velocity
member.summary: Saved movement velocity used when restoring a body that was awake before hibernation.

remarks.para: The vector gives movement along the scene's world X, Y and Z axes in units per second, normally metres per second in BONELAB. For example, (0, 2, 0) represents two metres per second upward.

CopyFrom updates it only when the body is not sleeping. CopyTo applies it and wakes the body only when the saved isSleeping flag is false. Capturing a sleeping body leaves this vector unchanged, so it can contain an older snapshot's value.
Editing it affects a later awake-state restoration, rather than moving the live body immediately. The restored constraints can still restrict that motion.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.MarrowEntity.HibernationSources.Culling
member.summary: Keeps an entity’s physics paused while the culling system marks it inactive.

remarks.para: A Rigidbody is Unity’s component that gives an object simulated movement and rotation. Culling means setting aside an entity that the culling system considers inactive. Hibernation pauses its physics bodies: for bodies with a Rigidbody, the routine saves their current physics state, freezes movement and rotation, and puts them to sleep. Culling is reason bit 2, separate from the Default and Loading reasons.

These are independent reason flags, not request counts. Hibernate(true, source) adds the selected reason bits; Hibernate(false, source) removes only those bits. The entity’s flags change first. Its body pause/restore work runs only when the overall state changes between no active reason and at least one active reason.

The ordinary OnCullResolve path adds the Culling reason before disabling the entity’s configured behaviours, its script components, then calls their registered cull handlers. A handler is a routine called to report the culling action. On unculling, it removes Culling first, enables the configured behaviours, then calls uncull handlers. Removing this reason restores body state only if no other hibernation reason remains.

For example, with both Culling and Loading active, Hibernate(false, Culling) leaves Loading active and the bodies remain paused. Using Culling as the source argument in a direct Hibernate call edits this reason; the behaviour and handler steps belong to the surrounding culling path.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.MarrowEntity.HibernationSources.Default
member.summary: Marks a general hibernation request, including Hibernate calls that omit the source argument.

remarks.para: A Rigidbody is Unity’s component that gives an object simulated movement and rotation. Default is active reason bit 1. It does not mean that no reason is set: an entity with this bit still counts as hibernating. Hibernate(true) uses Default when the caller omits the source, and Hibernate(false) likewise removes Default only. Culling or Loading reasons can remain active.

These are independent reason flags, not request counts. Hibernate(true, source) adds the selected reason bits; Hibernate(false, source) removes only those bits. The entity’s flags change first. Its body pause/restore work runs only when the overall state changes between no active reason and at least one active reason.

Hibernation pauses physics bodies with saved-state restoration when the last reason is removed. For a body with a Rigidbody, entry saves its physics state, freezes movement and rotation, and puts it to sleep. Restoration returns the saved settings and prior sleeping/awake state; it does not promise that every restored body starts moving.

The Hibernate transition between no active reason and at least one active reason also uses Default when forwarding a host entity’s pause or restore to packed parasite entities: other entities grouped under that host by Pack. Thus this reason is not limited to explicit calls from your own script. Repeatedly adding the same Default bit does not create a count; one removal clears that bit.
For example, add Default with Hibernate(true), then add Loading. Calling Hibernate(false) removes Default but leaves Loading, so the entity stays hibernating until Loading is removed too.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.MarrowEntity.HibernationSources.Loading
member.summary: Keeps spawned entity physics paused while a level-streaming load is in progress.

remarks.para: A Rigidbody is Unity’s component that gives an object simulated movement and rotation. Loading is active reason bit 4. The entity’s physics spawn path checks the SceneStreamer session; when its status is LOADING, it calls Hibernate(true, Loading). The level-load-complete routine calls Hibernate(false, Loading) to remove that reason.

These are independent reason flags, not request counts. Hibernate(true, source) adds the selected reason bits; Hibernate(false, source) removes only those bits. The entity’s flags change first. Its body pause/restore work runs only when the overall state changes between no active reason and at least one active reason.

For bodies with a Rigidbody, hibernation saves their physics state, freezes movement and rotation, and puts them to sleep. Removing the last active reason restores the saved body state. Completing a load removes Loading only; it does not clear Default or Culling and therefore does not guarantee that every entity’s physics is restored immediately.

For example, a spawned entity can have Loading | Culling active. Level-load completion removes Loading, leaving Culling and keeping the bodies paused until the culling system removes that reason. The bit is a loading reason, not a time duration or a separate count for each load request.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.MarrowLayers.BeingTracker
member.summary: Layer 27 for the trigger shapes generated by the Being tracker channel.

remarks.para: A GameObject is one object in a Unity scene. A collider supplies its collision/detection shape. A physics query asks which shapes match a search. A layer mask is the set of categories that search is allowed to consider. Each bit is a yes/no switch selecting one category. The << operator moves the on bit of 1 to the numbered position: 1 << 27 selects just layer 27, giving the single-layer mask 134217728. The mask is a unitless selection number, not the GameObject’s layer index.

A Tracker links an overlap-detection shape to a MarrowBody, the physical part, and its MarrowEntity, the object grouping those parts. Registered means that the Tracker is available in the game’s Tracker lookup. Tracker.Awake, Unity’s initialization callback (a routine called to perform or report an action), registers the Tracker and sets its cached hasBody and hasEntity flags from the body and entity references present then. Zone requires those two flags to be true; its overlap handler does not check the current validity of those references again. Tracker.Validate assigns the references without refreshing these flags.

When enabled tracker settings choose the Being channel, MarrowBody.GenerateTrackers reuses or creates a child Tracker, and Tracker.Validate assigns this layer to its object. Tracker validation creates or configures its BoxCollider, SphereCollider or CapsuleCollider as a trigger: a shape that detects overlaps rather than acting as a solid wall.

This is the unitless layer index 27, assigned with gameObject.layer = (int)MarrowLayers.BeingTracker. For a physics query that should include this category, use the mask 1 << 27; passing 27 as the mask selects a different set of layers. A GameObject has one layer, while a mask can include several.

Being is the selected tracking channel, not a runtime test that an object is alive. Generation follows the MarrowBody's tracker settings; layer 27 by itself does not identify a player, enemy or living character.

For example, a query mask containing 1 << 27 selects this channel's shapes. To receive a useful Zone entry, make the Tracker available in the lookup with its cached hasBody and hasEntity flags true, and configure the zone's trigger and collision rules; assigning the layer to an unrelated collider does not create that tracking setup.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.MarrowLayers.BeingTrigger
member.summary: Layer 30 for classifying a Being tracking volume separately from the shapes it detects.

remarks.para: A GameObject is one object in a Unity scene. A collider supplies its collision/detection shape. A physics query asks which shapes match a search. A layer mask is the set of categories that search is allowed to consider. Each bit is a yes/no switch selecting one category. The << operator moves the on bit of 1 to the numbered position: 1 << 30 selects just layer 30, giving the single-layer mask 1073741824. The mask is a unitless selection number, not the GameObject’s layer index.

A Tracker links an overlap-detection shape to a MarrowBody, the physical part, and its MarrowEntity, the object grouping those parts. Registered means that the Tracker is available in the game’s Tracker lookup. Tracker.Awake, Unity’s initialization callback (a routine called to perform or report an action), registers the Tracker and sets its cached hasBody and hasEntity flags from the body and entity references present then. Zone requires those two flags to be true; its overlap handler does not check the current validity of those references again. Tracker.Validate assigns the references without refreshing these flags.

This is the unitless layer index 30, assigned with gameObject.layer = (int)MarrowLayers.BeingTrigger. For a physics query that should include this category, use the mask 1 << 30; passing 30 as the mask selects a different set of layers. A GameObject has one layer, while a mask can include several.

The matching tracker category is BeingTracker, layer 27. To make a zone detect those shapes, configure a trigger collider and collision rules that let the two categories overlap. A trigger is a collider used for overlap detection rather than solid contact. Putting a GameObject on this layer does not add its collider or Zone component.

When Zone receives an overlap, it first tries to find the Tracker in its lookup using the overlapping collider's object. When that succeeds and the Zone is active and enabled, it requires the Tracker’s cached hasBody and hasEntity flags to be true before recording the entry. The layer is part of selecting which overlap pairs reach this logic; the number alone does not register an arbitrary collider as a tracked object.

For example, use 1 << 30 in a query mask to look for these volumes, or 1 << 27 when the query should look for their matching tracker shapes. Those are different categories; one is the detection volume and the other is the object being detected.

member.summary: Layer 17, keeping Deciverse-classified shapes separate from ordinary body colliders.

remarks.para: A GameObject is one object in a Unity scene. A collider supplies its collision/detection shape. A physics query asks which shapes match a search. A layer mask is the set of categories that search is allowed to consider. Each bit is a yes/no switch selecting one category. The << operator moves the on bit of 1 to the numbered position: 1 << 17 selects just layer 17, giving the single-layer mask 131072. The mask is a unitless selection number, not the GameObject’s layer index.

This is the unitless layer index 17, assigned with gameObject.layer = (int)MarrowLayers.Deciverse. For a physics query that should include this category, use the mask 1 << 17; passing 17 as the mask selects a different set of layers. A GameObject has one layer, while a mask can include several.

When MarrowBody gathers its ordinary body colliders, it preserves this existing layer instead of replacing it with Default or Dynamic. Assigning this category therefore keeps those gathered shapes distinct for layer-based collision filtering and queries; it does not change their size or add components.

For example, a query that includes 1 << 17 can consider a shape assigned to this category. The layer selects which shapes the query considers; any boundary response or transition must be supplied by the volume's components and configured collision rules.

The << operator moves the on bit of 1 to the numbered position: 1 << 0 selects just layer 0, giving the single-layer mask 1. Default being zero does not mean an empty query mask. Its mask is 1, because bit zero is set; a mask of 0 includes no layers. For example, a ray query with mask 1 can consider Default colliders, subject to the query's other options. Choosing Default alone does not freeze a Rigidbody or make a shape solid.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.OverlapTriggerManager.EventType.TriggerEnter
member.summary: Marks a queued overlap-start notification that calls OnOverlapEnter when processed.

remarks.para: A GameObject is an object in the Unity scene. A collider is a shape attached to it that Unity uses to detect contact. The counts group reported contacts by the two scene objects, so several colliders on the same object share a count. The queued record also contains an OverlapTrigger component and the other GameObject. When the manager drains the queue, this kind calls that component's OnOverlapEnter callback with the other object. A callback is a routine called to perform or report an action. This value labels the notification; it does not itself create a physical overlap.

Normal enter reporting queues this kind only when the trigger-GameObject and other-GameObject pair had no positive recorded count. It queues the notification, then increases the pair's count. The callback is dispatched through the manager's queue after that reporting work, rather than directly inside the collider enter report.

For example, the first reported contact between two GameObjects queues an enter, while another contact between colliders on those same GameObjects only increases the count. Different child GameObjects remain separate partners. Each queued record has one event kind; Enter and Exit are not flags to combine. Queue processing has no promised one-frame delay.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.OverlapTriggerManager.EventType.TriggerExit
member.summary: Marks a queued overlap-end notification that calls OnOverlapExit when processed.

remarks.para: A GameObject is an object in the Unity scene. A collider is a shape attached to it that Unity uses to detect contact. The counts group reported contacts by the two scene objects, so several colliders on the same object share a count. The queued record also contains an OverlapTrigger component and the other GameObject. Processing this kind calls that component's OnOverlapExit callback with the other object. A callback is a routine called to perform or report an action. It reports the end of a recorded relationship; it does not move the objects apart.

Normal exit reporting decreases the pair's recorded count first. While the count remains positive, it does not queue this kind. At the final count it queues exit notifications and removes the pair entry before the manager later dispatches the callbacks. DisableOverlap can generate the same kind by clearing all remaining recorded counts when an object is disabled, even if it never physically left the volume.

For example, with two reported contacts between the same two GameObjects, ending one leaves a positive count and produces no exit notification; ending the remaining one queues an exit. Each queued record selects one event kind, rather than combining Enter and Exit flags. Previously queued notifications are retained, and dispatch timing follows the manager's queue processing without an exact frame-delay promise.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.PolyLineData.SegmentResolution.Centimeter
member.summary: Uses a 0.01-unit spacing assumption for the line’s stored samples.

remarks.para: SegmentDistance returns 0.01 for this choice. The stored samples are points prepared ahead of time to describe the path; this is what a baked path means here. Local distances are measured in the line’s own coordinates before scene scaling. The baked-line reader uses this step in those local distance units. At unit scale, meaning no size scaling on the line or its parents, it corresponds to 1 centimeter. For evenly spaced samples, an illustrative 1-meter local length contains 100 intervals at this step.

GetPointAtLinearDistance divides the requested distance from its supplied position by this spacing to estimate where to start searching the stored polyVerts samples. That distance is a signed straight-line separation in the line’s own coordinates; its sign chooses the search direction. The setting must therefore describe how those samples were prepared. Selecting it alone does not add vertices or rebuild an existing baked path.

Awake, Unity’s initialization routine, copies this spacing into PolyLine when the data contains baked samples. Changing the asset’s enum afterward does not refresh an already initialized PolyLine’s cached spacing. Local spacing also does not automatically compensate for later scaling of the line in the scene.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.SoftSplineJointLimit.bounciness
member.summary: Controls how strongly the constrained body rebounds when it reaches the linear limit.

remarks.para: This is a unitless bounce amount. Unity’s documented range is 0 through 1: 0 adds no bounce at the boundary, while 1 is the most bouncy end of that range. Values between them give intermediate rebound. This is not a force in newtons, and it does not set the spring or damping strengths.

SplineJoint copies this setting into its generated physics connection during One-contact setup. Here a Contact is a generated physics helper connection, not a collision touch. One, Two and Four name how many such helpers are created. That connection is a ConfigurableJoint, which connects physical bodies and restricts their movement. Here Y and Z are the connection’s sideways axes, not fixed world directions. The Y/Z motion mode must be Limited for this sideways limit to matter; Locked motion prevents that movement instead. The Two- and Four-contact setup paths lock Y/Z and do not pass this configured setting.

The constructor stores the supplied number without clamping it. Existing joints retain the copy installed during setup when this struct is later edited; changing the stored number alone does not update those joint settings.

For example, with a limit of 0.05 meters (5 centimeters), contactDistance=0.01 gives a 1-centimeter region approaching that boundary in which the solver can prepare the limit response. The physics solver is the engine calculation that applies movement constraints and forces.

The buffer allows the engine to consider the limit before the object would cross it, which can help fast-moving bodies avoid passing the boundary. It changes when the constraint is considered, not the allowed boundary distance. Zero requests Unity’s default contact tolerance; it is not necessarily a zero-width buffer.

SplineJoint copies this setting into its generated physics connection during One-contact setup. Here a Contact is a generated physics helper connection, not a collision touch. The Two- and Four-contact setup paths lock Y/Z and do not pass this configured setting.

This is not a collision shape or a radius for finding nearby objects. The constructor stores it directly, and changing the struct after the joint has copied it does not automatically refresh that joint’s tolerance.

remarks.para: A contact is a generated physics anchor connected to the moving body by a joint, which constrains their relative movement. This choice sets that joint's Y and Z translation modes to Limited. Those axes run sideways to the path in the contact's joint frame; the choice does not set a travel range along the spline's X direction or select its rotational behavior.

The boundary comes from the joint's shared linear limit, a distance from the joint origin that restricts its limited translation axes. In SplineJoint's single-contact setup, the initial limit and its response settings come from _linearYZLimit. Its distance is measured in Unity scene distance units from the joint origin, not as a percentage of the spline. Limited permits bounded sideways offset instead of locking those translations; it does not guarantee the object will reach the boundary or choose a particular amount of movement.

SplineJoint.Attach passes the configured _linearYZMotion only for ContactCount.One. Its Two and Four layouts construct their contacts with Locked sideways motion, even if the configured choice is Limited. Choose the mode before Awake, Unity's initialization callback; a callback is a routine called to perform or report an action. Changing the field later does not automatically rebuild existing contacts, and RefreshContactConfig updates their drives rather than their Y/Z motion policies. Joint drives apply forces that push or turn the body toward target motion.

The single-contact endpoint handling can call Contact.LimitDirection, which replaces the same shared linear-distance limit while limiting X. That replacement also affects Y/Z while they remain Limited, so the initial sideways boundary is not promised to stay unchanged throughout travel. For a single-contact guide, this choice describes allowed sideways offset from the moving anchor, rather than a command to stop the body at a chosen point on the rail.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.SplineJointMotion.Locked
member.summary: Constrains sideways sliding at a generated spline contact by locking its Y and Z translation axes.

remarks.para: A generated contact is a physics anchor connected to the moving body by a joint, which constrains relative movement. Locked sets the joint's Y and Z translation modes to Locked. These are sideways axes in that joint's frame. The enum does not lock the body's progress along the spline's X direction or select its angular motion.

For example, a rail-guided body can use locked sideways translation while its separate X settings still allow or drive travel along the rail. This is a physics constraint choice, not a command to teleport the body onto the curve or freeze its complete position. Other joints, drives, rotation settings, and endpoint handling still affect the body. Joint drives apply forces that push or turn the body toward target motion.

SplineJoint's One-contact layout passes the configured _linearYZMotion into contact construction. Two and Four layouts use Locked sideways motion for every generated contact regardless of that field. Configure the choice before Awake, Unity's initialization callback; a callback is a routine called to perform or report an action. Editing the enum afterward does not automatically rewrite existing joints, and refreshing contact drives does not change these Y/Z motion policies.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.TrackerSettings.Direction.XAxis
member.summary: Capsule volume runs along the local X axis.

remarks.para: This selects the end-to-end axis of a capsule, a pill-shaped detection volume with rounded ends. Local X means the tracker collider GameObject's own left/right direction, rather than a fixed world axis. Rotating that object rotates this axis in the scene. For example, this choice can orient an elongated detection volume running from one side of the tracker to the other; its dimensions are supplied separately.

The choice is applied when Tracker.Validate processes a TrackerSettings entry whose type is Capsule. The generated collider is a trigger, which detects overlaps rather than provides a solid surface. Bounds, Box, and Sphere branches of that validation routine do not use this direction choice to orient their shapes.

Set TrackerSettings.direction before body validation or tracker generation applies the entry. GenerateTrackers processes active entries and calls tracker validation to create or reuse the collider. Editing the enum value alone changes the settings data rather than immediately changing an existing CapsuleCollider; the validation path must apply it again. Choose one axis, rather than combining these values as flags.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.TrackerSettings.Type.Bounds
member.summary: Fits a box-shaped tracking trigger from the body’s bounds without compensating for the tracker’s scale.

remarks.para: Despite the name, this selects a BoxCollider. Its requested center and full X/Y/Z side lengths come from MarrowBody.Bounds, not from TrackerSettings.center or TrackerSettings.size. The body’s bounds are the saved box enclosing its colliders, with the body’s current scale applied. The center is an offset relative to the body, not an absolute position in the world. CalculateBounds produces this cached enclosing geometry. GenerateTrackers and Tracker.Validate use that saved geometry with the body’s current scale; they do not remeasure the colliders or call CalculateBounds during tracker validation.

Those center and size numbers are copied directly into the tracker collider’s local coordinates, meaning coordinates relative to the tracker object’s origin and axes. Unity then applies the tracker’s own transform scale to that collider. Unlike Box, this option does not divide out that scale. For an illustrative positive uniform tracker scale of 2, a requested side length of 1 becomes a 1-unit local side and a 2-unit world side; Box would request a 0.5-unit local side instead. Unity distance units normally represent meters.

Validation compares the lengths of the old and requested center vectors, and separately the lengths of the size vectors. A center vector’s length is the straight-line distance from the collider’s origin to its center. A size vector’s length is sqrt(sizeX² + sizeY² + sizeZ²), where sizeX, sizeY and sizeZ are the complete side lengths in local distance units. This check combines all three sides rather than comparing each side independently. It writes each vector only when those lengths differ by more than 0.0001 local distance units. A different center direction or different side proportions with the same vector length can therefore leave the old collider value in place.

A collider is a shape Unity uses for physics detection. GenerateTrackers processes this settings entry only when its isActive flag is enabled. Bounds also requires at least one gathered ordinary body collider; the other three shape choices can proceed without one. This choice is read when MarrowBody.GenerateTrackers sets up the tracking shapes through Tracker.Validate. Changing the enum alone does not replace an existing collider. Validation checks only the first Collider returned by GetComponent on the tracker object. It reuses that component only when its kind matches; otherwise it adds the selected kind without removing the old component. It does not search later colliders for a match, so another matching collider can still be added when the first one has a different kind. The selected collider is made a trigger: it reports overlaps rather than acting as a solid wall. The separate layer setting chooses the tracking category.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.TrackerSettings.Type.Box
member.summary: Fits a box-shaped tracking trigger from the body’s bounds while compensating for the tracker’s scale.

remarks.para: The requested center and full X/Y/Z side lengths come from MarrowBody.Bounds, the body’s saved enclosing box with its current scale applied. TrackerSettings.center and TrackerSettings.size are not read for this option. The center is a relative offset, not an absolute world position, and size gives complete side lengths rather than half-widths. CalculateBounds produces this cached enclosing geometry. GenerateTrackers and Tracker.Validate use that saved geometry with the body’s current scale; they do not remeasure the colliders or call CalculateBounds during tracker validation.

Validation divides each center and size component by the matching component of the tracker’s lossyScale: its combined scale, including parents. These scale factors have no units; 1 means unchanged size and 2 means twice the size. The result is assigned in the collider’s local axes, which rotate with the tracker. For example, with a requested 1-meter side and a positive uniform tracker scale of 2, the collider receives a 0.5-unit local side and the transform scales it back to 1 meter. Bounds copies the requested side directly instead.

Validation compares the lengths of the old and requested center vectors, and separately the lengths of the size vectors. A center vector’s length is the straight-line distance from the collider’s origin to its center. A size vector’s length is sqrt(sizeX² + sizeY² + sizeZ²), where sizeX, sizeY and sizeZ are the complete side lengths in local distance units. This check combines all three sides rather than comparing each side independently. It writes each vector only when those lengths differ by more than 0.0001 local distance units. A different center direction or different side proportions with the same vector length can therefore leave the old collider value in place.

This shape choice can proceed even when no ordinary body colliders were gathered. This choice is read when MarrowBody.GenerateTrackers sets up the tracking shapes through Tracker.Validate. Changing the enum alone does not replace an existing collider. Validation checks only the first Collider returned by GetComponent on the tracker object. It reuses that component only when its kind matches; otherwise it adds the selected kind without removing the old component. member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.TrackerSettings.Type.Capsule
member.summary: Uses the configured center, radius, total height and axis to create a rounded tracking trigger.

remarks.para: A capsule is a cylinder with a rounded end at each end. center is an offset from the tracker origin along its axes; radius is the distance from the long axis to the side; height is the total end-to-end length, including the rounded ends. At scale 1, these distances normally use meters: for example, radius=0.1 gives a 20-centimeter diameter and height=0.6 gives a 60-centimeter total length. direction selects the tracker’s local long axis: XAxis = 0, YAxis = 1 or ZAxis = 2; it does not always mean vertical in the world.

Validation divides each center component by the matching component of the tracker’s combined scale, including parents. It multiplies both radius and height by the largest of the three reciprocal scale components. A reciprocal scale component means 1 divided by that axis’s scale factor; take the largest of the three results. A scale factor is unitless: 1 leaves size unchanged, and 2 doubles it. With positive uniform scale 2, this conversion halves the local center, radius and height before the transform scales the shape. With unequal axis scales, the same largest reciprocal is used for both lengths, so do not read the configured numbers as a guarantee of those exact world dimensions.

Validation writes the center only when the old and requested center-vector lengths differ by more than 0.0001 local distance units. A center vector’s length is the straight-line distance from the collider’s origin to its center. A change of direction with the same center-vector length can be skipped. Radius changes are written only when their difference exceeds 0.0001 local distance units. The same difference check applies to height; direction is assigned during validation.

A collider is a shape Unity uses for physics detection. GenerateTrackers processes this settings entry only when its isActive flag is enabled. This shape choice can proceed even when no ordinary body colliders were gathered. This choice is read when MarrowBody.GenerateTrackers sets up the tracking shapes through Tracker.Validate. Changing the enum alone does not replace an existing collider. Validation checks only the first Collider returned by GetComponent on the tracker object. It reuses that component only when its kind matches; otherwise it adds the selected kind without removing the old component. It does not search later colliders for a match, so another matching collider can still be added when the first one has a different kind. The selected collider is made a trigger: it reports overlaps rather than acting as a solid wall. The separate layer setting chooses the tracking category.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.TrackerSettings.Type.Sphere
member.summary: Uses the configured center and radius to create a spherical tracking trigger.

remarks.para: center is the offset from the tracker’s origin along its axes, and radius is the distance from the sphere’s center to its surface. At scale 1, these distances normally use meters. For example, radius=0.25 describes a 50-centimeter diameter. TrackerSettings.size, height and direction are not used for this shape.

Validation divides each center component by the matching component of the tracker’s combined scale, including parents. It multiplies radius by the largest reciprocal scale component. A reciprocal scale component means 1 divided by that axis’s scale factor; take the largest of the three results. These scale factors are unitless: 1 leaves size unchanged and 2 doubles it. For positive uniform scale 2, a configured radius of 0.25 becomes a local collider radius of 0.125, which the transform scales back to 0.25 meters. Unequal axis scales still use that one largest reciprocal; the configured radius is not a guarantee of the same world radius under that scaling.

Validation writes the center only when the old and requested center-vector lengths differ by more than 0.0001 local distance units. A center vector’s length is the straight-line distance from the collider’s origin to its center. A change of direction with the same center-vector length can be skipped. Radius changes are written only when their difference exceeds 0.0001 local distance units.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.InteractionOptions.FarHover
member.summary: Allows a Grip to be considered as a target in the hand’s distant-hover search.

remarks.para: Far-hover means pointing toward a grip beyond the normal nearby-hand candidate search. The receiver is the component accepting hand interactions; its host is the object the grip belongs to. Hand.UpdateHovering considers this route when it has no nearby target and the hand’s far-hover feature is enabled. The candidate receiver must be enabled, its grippable host must allow far-hover, and this option must be present. The search still checks aim and obstruction, and rejects the object already held by the other hand. Enabling this flag alone therefore does not make every distant grip selectable.

This flag permits selection and the corresponding far-hover notifications; it does not itself move the object or attach a hand. A listener is registered code called when a notification occurs, with the reporting Hand. When the hand changes its far-hover target, the old receiver's end callback runs before the hand stores the new receiver; the new receiver's begin callback runs after that update. For example, ForcePullGrip.Enable adds this flag and registers listeners for the grip’s far-hover begin, end and update notifications. Its update listener can start the pull sequence when the host is unattached and one primary/secondary interaction button is newly pressed while the other is held. ForcePullGrip’s startup also enables far-hover on the host. Those additional pieces supply the pull action.

The flag’s value is 4. Add it with a bitwise OR to preserve the other options; clearing only this flag preserves them too. ForcePullGrip.Enable and Disable perform that add/remove themselves, so a separate edit to the grip options can be changed by that component’s later calls. Changing the enum value alone does not register a pull listener or enable the host’s far-hover feature.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.InteractionOptions.MultipleHands
member.summary: Allows the nearby-hover search to consider a grip that the other hand is already holding.

remarks.para: A receiver is the component that accepts hand interactions, and its GameObject is the scene object that carries it. Normally Hand.UpdateHovering skips a nearby receiver whose GameObject is the same object held by the other hand. With MultipleHands on that candidate Grip, the search can score it alongside other candidates. This supports selecting the same grip with both hands instead of rejecting it solely because the other hand already has it. Availability, shape and distance checks still apply; enabling the flag does not attach a second hand automatically.

The flag’s value is 1. For example, a grip intended for both hands can include MultipleHands while leaving SwitchHands clear. If SwitchHands is also present, Hand.AttachObject still force-detaches that grip’s existing hands before recording the new attachment; MultipleHands does not cancel that separate transfer behavior. Clearing MultipleHands later changes subsequent candidate selection, rather than immediately detaching hands already attached.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.InteractionOptions.SwitchHands
member.summary: Makes attachment to this grip release its existing hands before the new hand is attached.

remarks.para: Hand.AttachObject first detaches the incoming hand from its current object. If the target Grip has SwitchHands, it then calls that grip’s quick ForceDetach path for its already attached hands. Only afterward does it store the incoming hand’s new attached-object reference and run the new receiver’s attachment handling. This gives a transfer to the new hand instead of keeping the old hands attached to that grip.

The flag’s value is 8. For example, a grip can use this behavior when attachment by the right hand should release its existing left-hand hold. This takes effect when attachment is actually requested; merely changing the option does not transfer the object. It also does not make an otherwise unavailable grip pass hover selection. The nearby-hover search has its separate MultipleHands gate for a target already held by the other hand. If both flags are set, the candidate can pass that gate, but the attachment path still releases its existing hands.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.InteractionOptions.ToggledGrip
member.summary: Enables Vive-wand handling that keeps a grip held through the initial secondary-button release and releases it on a later one.

remarks.para: In Grip.OnHandAttachedUpdate, this special path requires both ToggledGrip and a controller whose Type is ViveWands. Other controller types still use their ordinary IsReleased result even when this flag is set. In the Vive-wand path, the tested input is GetSecondaryInteractionButtonUp: the controller’s report that its secondary interaction button has just been released. It is a release-edge test, rather than a universal button-press toggle for every controller.

OnAttachedToHand sets hasStartedToGrip for that combination. This is a grip-wide latch, meaning a remembered true/false flag for the initial attachment input. For this ViveWands path, the attached-hand callback runs before the latch is set, so a listener reading it during that callback sees its previous value. While the latch is true, a secondary-button release does not run this release path. A held update clears the latch when the secondary button is no longer held. Once it is clear, a later secondary-button release requests detachment. For example, the initial grab can survive letting go of that input; using and releasing the secondary input again then releases the grip. The latch is shared by the grip, rather than a separate toggle record for every hand.

The flag’s value is 2. When SkeletonHand is not moving the hand toward a target, this Vive-wand option requests full-curl targets for the thumb, middle, ring and pinky fingers. It leaves the index finger on its normal supplied curl input. The finger animation approaches these targets smoothly; this is not a promise that the whole hand instantly becomes fully curled. This changes the visual pose, rather than which button edge causes release. Assigning this option does not attach anything immediately, and it does not prevent other force-detach or disable cleanup paths from releasing a grip.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.LadderInfo.Source.FEET
member.summary: Foot-contact category in a ladder report, with numeric value 2.

remarks.para: The checked PhysGrounder foot-collision path requests this category after ladder checking is enabled, the collided object matches the PhysGrounder's configured collisionLayer, and it has a live LadderPlatform linked to a ladder controller. A physics layer is a group used to filter objects for collision checks. The report is then sent to PhysicsRig.UpdateLadderInfo.

That update stores the report before setting the rig’s onLadder flag to 1. The report carries the ladder’s rung reference and dimensions for movement assistance; the enum value alone does not run collision detection or put a foot on a rung.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.LadderInfo.Source.LEFTHAND
member.summary: Left-hand category in a ladder report, with numeric value 0.

remarks.para: LadderVirtualController.GetLadderInfo stores this value when it is supplied as the source argument. The checked controller physics-update path also uses value 0 when reporting its selected attached hand to PhysicsRig.UpdateLadderInfo. A physics update is a step of the movement and collision simulation.

That path uses the same value without testing whether the selected hand is left or right, so this label is not proof that a left-hand grip was detected. Selecting it does not attach a hand or animate fingers. The rig update stores the report first, then marks onLadder as 1.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.LadderInfo.Source.RIGHTHAND
member.summary: Right-hand category in a ladder report, with numeric value 1.

remarks.para: Passing RIGHTHAND to LadderVirtualController.GetLadderInfo copies this value into the returned report along with the ladder’s rung reference and dimensions. PhysicsRig.UpdateLadderInfo can store that report and then mark onLadder as 1.

This identifies the supplied category; it does not itself detect or attach a right hand. The checked controller physics-update reporter writes value 0 for its selected attached hand rather than choosing this value from handedness. The checked LadderForce assistance routine uses the stored rung information and does not branch on this category.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.OpenControllerRig.CurveMode.Dpad
member.summary: Selects the configured curve_Dpad curve as the active controller-direction mapping.

remarks.para: OnStart, the rig’s startup routine, selects this preset when curveMode is Dpad; SetTouchPadCurve(Dpad) selects it immediately. The selector copies the existing curve_Dpad reference into touchPadCurve. It does not create a curve, edit its keys or update the saved curveMode.

The selected curve maps the input angle from upward input, positive toward the right and measured in degrees, to an output direction angle in degrees. This angular-mapping stage keeps the unitless deflection magnitude supplied to it; earlier input processing can change that magnitude. For example, a configured key mapping 30 degrees to 45 degrees changes direction without changing how far the control is deflected.

The assigned AnimationCurve keys determine the actual response. The name Dpad does not by itself guarantee identity mapping (keeping the same direction), cardinal snapping (snapping to up, right, down or left), digital steps (only fixed direction steps) or time filtering (smoothing changes over time). Configure the desired angle-mapping points (keys) on the corresponding AnimationCurve; replacing that curve object after selection requires selecting it again to replace the active reference.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.OpenControllerRig.DirectionMode.Controller
member.summary: Selects the non-dominant physical controller as the orientation reference for walking.

remarks.para: With isRightHanded true, this selects the physical left controller transform; with the flag false, it selects physical right. OnStart and SetDirectionMasterTransform copy that transform into directionMasterTransform. The physical tracked hands are not exchanged.

OnEarlyUpdate uses the selected world orientation together with the body-support reference to rotate active, unitless movement-axis input. For example, changing the selected controller’s facing changes the direction supplied by the same walking input. This chooses a direction source, not a destination or a speed in metres per second.

Changing the saved directionMode or handedness alone does not automatically rebuild the current direction reference. Select Controller again when a changed handedness should choose the other hand. BodyVitals.PROPEGATE_SOFT, the routine that copies player settings into the rig, selects direction before copying its new handedness into the rig, so that path can initially use the earlier hand choice.

A Transform stores an object’s position, rotation and scale. Here the selected world rotation is compared with centerOfPressure, the rig Transform used as the body’s orientation base, before turning the walking input.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.OpenControllerRig.TrackedState.BlendingToTracked
member.summary: On the left/right controller path, applies a fading pose correction while moving the output toward the supplied tracked pose. The headset uses separate pose handling and does not run this fade sequence.

remarks.para: The rig enters this state when its pose-handling routine changes to tracked input. It first snapshots the difference between the current output and the new target, performs an initial blend step, then stores BlendingToTracked. This lets the current displayed pose approach the tracked target without an immediate jump at the change.

While tracked input continues, later calls fade the stored correction. Its position is a displacement in local distance units in the output parent’s axes, its rotation is an orientation difference, and the remaining blend weight is unitless. When the weight is at or below 0.01, the routine sets the weight to zero before changing the state to Tracked.

For example, reconnecting a controller at a different pose can temporarily retain part of that difference while the hand moves toward the supplied target. If tracking is lost during this transition, the routine takes a new snapshot from the current output and changes to BlendingToUntracked; that loss-side blend starts on a later call. The enum is pose-transition state, not a request to reconnect the device.

Position uses distance units in the output parent’s axes, relative to the object containing the output. These normally correspond to metres when the parent chain has scale 1; scaling that chain changes the corresponding world distance. For example, a local displacement of 0.10 is 10 cm at scale 1, or 20 cm along an axis with cumulative parent scale 2.

The blend weight is the unitless amount used when BlendOffset applies a saved pose correction. A pose calculation using weight 1 applies the full saved position and orientation difference; as that applied weight falls toward 0 less correction remains, and a calculation using weight 0 leaves the supplied target.

At completion, BlendOffset writes the last small correction first. The routine then clears the stored weight and changes state, without rewriting the pose after that clear. The output can therefore retain a small correction despite the new stored zero; the next steady-state call copies the tracked target directly. For example, an applied weight of 0.005 with a saved displacement of 0.10 local distance units leaves 0.0005 local distance units of correction even though the stored weight is then cleared. These are illustrative values, not a fixed number of frames or a device guarantee.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.OpenControllerRig.TrackedState.BlendingToUntracked
member.summary: On the left/right controller path, applies a fading pose correction while moving the output toward the supplied tracking fallback. The headset uses separate pose handling and does not run this fade sequence.

remarks.para: When tracked input is lost, the pose-handling routine snapshots the difference from the current output to the fallback target, then stores BlendingToUntracked. It does not perform the first loss-side BlendOffset step in that entry branch; subsequent untracked calls advance the blend.

The fallback is the caller’s target, such as a remembered controller pose reconstructed relative to the head, rather than a guaranteed fixed rest pose. The stored positional difference uses local distance units, the rotation is an orientation difference, and the remaining blend weight is unitless. At a weight at or below 0.01, the routine writes zero to the weight before changing the state to Untracked.

For example, a controller losing tracking can keep part of its previous placement while blending toward the head-relative fallback. If tracked input returns during the transition, the routine snapshots again from the current output, performs an initial tracked-side blend step, then changes to BlendingToTracked. Setting the enum alone does not sample or repair a device.

Position uses distance units in the output parent’s axes, relative to the object containing the output. These normally correspond to metres when the parent chain has scale 1; scaling that chain changes the corresponding world distance. For example, a local displacement of 0.10 is 10 cm at scale 1, or 20 cm along an axis with cumulative parent scale 2.

The blend weight is the unitless amount used when BlendOffset applies a saved pose correction. A pose calculation using weight 1 applies the full saved position and orientation difference; as that applied weight falls toward 0 less correction remains, and a calculation using weight 0 leaves the supplied target.

At completion, BlendOffset writes the last small correction first. The routine then clears the stored weight and changes state, without rewriting the pose after that clear. The output can therefore retain a small correction despite the new stored zero; the next steady-state call copies the current fallback target directly. For example, an applied weight of 0.005 with a saved displacement of 0.10 local distance units leaves 0.0005 local distance units of correction even though the stored weight is then cleared. These are illustrative values, not a fixed number of frames or a device guarantee.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.OpenControllerRig.TrackedState.Tracked
member.summary: For controller outputs, applies the supplied tracked pose directly; the headset stores this value but uses separate pose handling.

remarks.para: For left and right controller outputs, ProcessTrackedBlend writes the supplied target’s local position and rotation to its output without starting a new tracking-transition correction. The position uses local distance units relative to the output parent; the rotation is its orientation in that parent’s axes. Other upstream filtering or pose checks can already have affected the supplied target.

If a controller's tracked argument becomes false, the routine snapshots the difference between the current output and the new fallback target, then changes to BlendingToUntracked. The blend toward that fallback begins on a later untracked controller call.

For example, a normally tracked controller hand follows the target the rig supplies, while a loss changes its state into the fallback transition. The same enum value is also stored in _headsetState: OnEarlyUpdate writes the tracked headset pose and updates that state on a separate path without calling ProcessTrackedBlend. In the controller helper, the enum is software pose state, not a guarantee of a fresh sensor sample, and assigning it does not poll the device.

For controller outputs, position uses distance units in the output parent’s axes, relative to the object containing the output. These normally correspond to metres when the parent chain has scale 1; scaling that chain changes the corresponding world distance. For example, a local displacement of 0.10 is 10 cm at scale 1, or 20 cm along an axis with cumulative parent scale 2.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.OpenControllerRig.TrackedState.Untracked
member.summary: For controller outputs, uses the supplied fallback pose until tracking returns; the headset uses a separate saved-pose path.

remarks.para: For left and right controller outputs, ProcessTrackedBlend writes the caller’s fallback target to the output’s local position and rotation. That target can move: the checked controller fallback is reconstructed from a remembered head-relative pose. It is not necessarily a stationary rest pose or the last world position.

When controller tracked input becomes true, the routine snapshots the current output’s difference from the new tracked target, performs an initial blend step, then changes to BlendingToTracked. This preserves continuity at the start of recovery.

For example, an untracked controller hand can continue following its head-relative fallback as the head turns. The same enum value is also stored in _headsetState: when the headset is untracked, OnEarlyUpdate writes the saved _lastHmdLocal pose (position and rotation relative to its parent) and resets that state; headset reacquisition uses separate handling rather than ProcessTrackedBlend. The enum records software pose state; assigning it does not disconnect or sample a device.

For controller outputs, position uses distance units in the output parent’s axes, relative to the object containing the output. These normally correspond to metres when the parent chain has scale 1; scaling that chain changes the corresponding world distance. For example, a local displacement of 0.10 is 10 cm at scale 1, or 20 cm along an axis with cumulative parent scale 2.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.OpenControllerRig.VrVertState.Crouch
member.summary: Crouching category for a lowered body with bent knees.

remarks.para: This is the Crouch label, with numeric value 1, in OpenControllerRig.vrVertState. It identifies a posture category; the label alone does not confirm that the avatar has reached that pose or is touching a supporting surface.

The complete inspected OpenControllerRig initialization, input, tracking, camera and body-update methods do not read or write vrVertState to choose a posture. Assigning this label is therefore not an established automatic pose command in those methods. That checked scope does not establish what every external script or saved scene may do with the field.

Keep this enum separate from RemapRig.VertState, which has a different numeric map and a separate field. For example, integer 2 is Sit here but Kneel in RemapRig.VertState; integer 3 is Kneel here but Prone there. Translate the intended category explicitly instead of casting the whole enums as if their values matched.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.PhysHand.HandPhysState.Empty
member.summary: This hand has no live grab joint in the latest hand-state classification.

remarks.para: A grab joint connects the hand to the object or fixed point it holds in the physics simulation. RefreshHandStates selects Empty when this hand’s joint is absent or destroyed, even if the other hand still has a grab.
This describes the grab connection, rather than requiring the hand to be motionless or free of collisions. RefreshHandStates overwrites the recorded state from the supplied joints.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.PhysHand.HandPhysState.RbOneHand
member.summary: This hand grips a dynamic Rigidbody without both hands sharing that same dynamic body.

remarks.para: A grab joint is the physics connection between the hand and the target it holds. A Rigidbody is an object’s simulated physical body. Dynamic here means its isKinematic flag is false, so physics forces can move it. RefreshHandStates selects this state when this hand’s joint connects to that kind of body and the other hand is empty, fixed, or attached to a different dynamic body.
For example, holding two separate dynamic objects gives each hand RbOneHand. Merely having both hands occupied does not select RbTwoHand. The state is refreshed from the actual grab joints.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.PhysHand.HandPhysState.RbTwoHand
member.summary: Both hands’ grab joints connect to the same dynamic Rigidbody.

remarks.para: A grab joint is the physics connection between the hand and the target it holds. A Rigidbody is the simulated physical body; dynamic here means isKinematic is false, so physics forces can move that body. RefreshHandStates assigns this state to both hands only when both live joints connect to that same body.

For example, two grips on one physical object can qualify, while one object in each hand does not. The comparison uses the connected Rigidbody, rather than the grips’ names or where the hands appear visually.

In the checked ApplyTorque path, this state halves the estimated rotational inertia used by that hand’s calculation. Rotational inertia describes how difficult it is to change an object’s spinning motion; this adjustment is part of the hand’s torque calculation. Torque is a turning force.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.PhysHand.HandPhysState.StaticOneHand
member.summary: This hand grips a fixed target while the other hand is empty or grips a dynamic body.

remarks.para: A Rigidbody is an object’s simulated physical body. A dynamic body can move under physics forces. A grab joint connects the hand to its target in the physics simulation. This target is classified as fixed when the joint has no connected Rigidbody or its connected body is kinematic, meaning motion is controlled outside normal force simulation.

If both hands have fixed targets, RefreshHandStates selects StaticTwoHand instead. If this hand is fixed and the other holds a dynamic object, their states are StaticOneHand and RbOneHand respectively. This is refreshed classification of the supplied joints.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.PhysHand.HandPhysState.StaticTwoHand
member.summary: Both hands have grab joints targeting fixed points or kinematic bodies.

remarks.para: A grab joint is the physics connection between the hand and its held target. A Rigidbody is an object’s simulated physical body. Each joint is treated as fixed when it has no connected Rigidbody or its connected body is kinematic, meaning normal physics forces do not determine that body’s motion.

The two targets do not have to be the same body or surface. RefreshHandStates assigns this state to both hands whenever both supplied grab joints are live and classified as fixed. Setting a state value does not create those grab connections.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.PhysicsRig.BodyMassState.Natural
member.summary: Mass layout used for the ordinary leg-based body, with a small knee/foot allocation.

remarks.para: Ball locomotion supports movement with the rig’s simulated knee and foot pair, separate from the visible leg limbs. The rig is the set of simulated body parts that controls the avatar’s physical movement. A Rigidbody is Unity’s component for a body with simulated mass, movement and collisions.

Let M be the avatar’s massTotal in kilograms and L its massLeg value in kilograms for one leg. Each arm receives A = 0.07317 × M kilograms. This mode assigns B = 0.02 × M kilograms to the simulated knee/foot pair, and the torso receives M − B − 2 × A − 2 × L kilograms. The multipliers are unitless; the factors of two account for two arms and two legs.

The foot Rigidbody receives 0.5625 × B kilograms and the knee Rigidbody receives 0.4375 × B kilograms. These unitless fractions divide the pair’s allocation into 56.25% and 43.75%. For an illustrative M of 100 kilograms, B is 2 kilograms: 1.125 for the foot and 0.875 for the knee.

The normal mass-state check selects this mode when ball locomotion is disabled and RigManager has no live active Seat. It sets the state before applying the mass distribution; the enum value does not remove physical joints (physics connections between bodies) or create an unconstrained body.

These budgets are applied when SetBodyMassDistribution runs. The separate leg limbs are also assigned the avatar’s massLeg value in every declared mode. Changing the state field alone does not execute that routine, and later automatic state checks can replace the field value.

Monofoot is the locomotion system using the rig’s simulated knee and foot bodies. Let M be the avatar’s massTotal in kilograms. Each arm receives A = 0.07317 × M kilograms, the knee/foot pair receives B = 0.12 × M kilograms, and the torso receives M − B − 2 × A kilograms. All multipliers are unitless; the factor of two accounts for two arms.

The foot receives 0.5625 × B kilograms and the knee receives 0.4375 × B kilograms, using unitless fractions. For an illustrative M of 100 kilograms, the pair receives 12 kilograms: 6.75 for the foot and 5.25 for the knee.

The normal mass-state check uses this mode while ball locomotion is enabled and can switch between it and StableMono as support conditions change. bodyMassNaturalHold keeps an existing NaturalMono state from switching to StableMono in that check.

These budgets are applied when SetBodyMassDistribution runs. The separate leg limbs are also each assigned massLeg, the avatar’s stored mass for one leg in kilograms, in every declared mode. Changing the state field alone does not execute that routine, and later automatic state checks can replace the field value.
