Pausing, completion, and forced reset have different effects on NPCs and asynchronous tasks; completion alone does not cancel the spawn loops. SERIES cancellation selects the preceding slot after progress advances. The music cue also has automatic timed release, so a looping clip is not a guarantee of music for the entire encounter.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.AI.SpawnAISettings
member.summary: Applies an enemy profile, home location, alert setting, and optional roaming override to NPCs when they spawn and reactivate.

remarks.para: It finds AIBrain on the spawned GameObject and applies settings through its navigation behaviour. A valid profile is applied first, then sound/home settings, then enabled roaming. OnSpawn also subscribes the post-reactivation callback; its death handler removes that callback and its own death listener.

The component supplies setup values rather than continuously driving every field each frame. ZONE modes use a RoamArea, WAYPOINTS uses transformed spline knots or waypoint objects, and LEGACY uses a home-centered rectangle with a subtracted offset. The geometry helpers build/copy separate setup data; changing a helper list or field does not automatically update an already configured NPC.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.AI.SpawnGroup
member.summary: An encounter’s serializable group of spawners, NPC tracking sets, count targets, and completion callbacks.

remarks.para: A callback is a routine called to perform or report an action. Here the group stores those routines so spawn, death, resurrection or completion notifications can trigger the matching work.

A SpawnGroup is a settings and tracking object, not a Unity component to attach to a GameObject. Its CrateSpawners and SpawnAISettings are scene components. Encounter’s normal and warmup loops use the group’s counters and limits to decide when to request NPCs; Setup connects the group to spawn notifications.

Successful NPC registration attaches death/resurrection listeners and classifies brains as alive or dead. Death history decides completion, while the current dead set decides corpse retention. Delayed removal can stop tracking a brain before its body disappears. Calling a spawn method directly does not automatically apply the encounter’s population gates or waits.

Cleanup clears tracking and unregisters spawners; it does not physically remove NPCs or cancel encounter tasks. Completion has its own latch and event order. The inspected bulk DespawnAllBrains helper also has an array-copy limitation: it copies dead and living sets to the same array starting at index zero, so mixed populations can overwrite entries and leave empty slots. Do not treat a force-stop notification as proof that every NPC was successfully removed.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.AI.TriggerRefProxy
member.summary: Connects a contacted physics body to character identity, an NPC brain, and the body points that AI targeting commands read.

remarks.para: GenGameControl_Trigger looks for this component on an entering collider’s attached Rigidbody GameObject, then uses triggerType to dispatch player or NPC events. It does not search root for the proxy. For Npc category, the proxy’s Start callback looks for AIBrain on root and caches it. A callback is a routine called to perform or report an action; this startup routine prepares the brain reference.

Configure the category, root and relevant body references before the component starts. targetHead supplies a live world-position point for AI direction/distance checks; feetTran supplies the position snapshot used by group investigation commands. This component does not create the referenced rig, physics bodies or markers.

NPC identity and team fields affect particular threat-scoring rules; they are not universal immunity or instant-aggression controls. The inspected runtime code does not establish special trigger-volume priority for chest, hand or head references.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.AI.TriggerRefProxy.NpcType
member.summary: Flags that label an NPC for threat scoring and select which NPC identities may pass an AI’s trigger-entry filter.

remarks.para: A flags enum assigns a different binary bit to each named value, allowing several values to be combined with |. BehaviourBaseNav.agroOnNpcType uses this as a permitted-identity mask. The inspected OnTriggerEnter accepts a non-Player candidate only when every bit in the candidate’s TriggerRefProxy.npcType is present in that mask. Player-category candidates bypass this identity-mask check.

For example, agroOnNpcType = NullBody | Crablet permits candidates labelled either NullBody or Crablet. A candidate itself labelled NullBody | Crablet requires both bits to be allowed; a mask containing only NullBody does not admit that combined value. These are label and mask examples, not default settings. A successful match lets the sensor consider the candidate with AddThreat; it does not guarantee an attack.

The identity-scoring functions use a different comparison. SubBehaviourSensors.InitialThreat returns zero for exactly equal whole npcType values and a distance-based score for different values. TriggerRefProxyUtilities.HostilityTowards also uses whole-value equality in its scoring rules. Two different combined values are not equal merely because they share one bit. Additional threat can still be added after the initial score.

Set TriggerRefProxy.npcType to label the existing character, and use BehaviourBaseNav.agroOnNpcType to configure the permitted mask. These labels do not load a prefab or change the NPC’s body, weapons or movement settings. Changing them does not clear threat already recorded by the sensors.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.AI.TriggerRefProxy.TriggerType
member.summary: Selects which trigger events a character proxy can produce and whether it supplies an NPC brain to AI consumers.

remarks.para: Player, Proxy and Npc are mutually exclusive category values, not flags to combine. The inspected GenGameControl_Trigger enter/exit handlers dispatch player events for Player and allowed NPC events for Npc, then optionally disable their trigger collider. Proxy matches neither branch.

For Npc, TriggerRefProxy.Start caches AIBrain from the root GameObject, and aiManager exposes it. Start is Unity’s startup callback: a routine called before the component’s first frame update. The other categories return null from aiManager. Configure category and root before that startup call; changing them later does not automatically repeat brain discovery.

The label changes consumer routing, not the character’s model, physics rig or controls. In particular, Proxy is not automatically a safe generic AI target because the sampled non-Player sensor path still requires a brain.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.AlignPlug
member.summary: Guides a held plug toward nearby sockets, seats it, and supports animated or physically guided removal.

remarks.para: A socket provides a place to insert the plug. Configure the plug and socket hosts, Marrow physics components and the socket’s insertion endpoint. The insertion direction is socket-local +X, its right axis; positions are usually meters when the objects have unit scale. An endpoint transform specifies a final position and facing, or endDistance gives the inward distance along that axis.

Nearby hover notifications fill the candidate list. While the plug is held, the hand update chooses a socket, requests a gradual hand-pose correction and starts insertion when the position and angle checks pass. The per-frame Update then aligns the plug with the mouth and moves it to the endpoint. ForceInSocket bypasses those checks and seats it immediately.

With configured socket and plug proxy grips, grabbing or requesting ejection can animate the plug out and transfer the hand to the plug grip. A seated host grabbed directly on a socket without a proxy grip instead receives a guide joint, a physics connection limiting its movement. ClearFromSocket provides immediate cleanup without an exit-complete hook.

Completion hooks are overridable methods called at specific points: insertion completion comes before the mass refresh, while animated exit completion comes after unlocking, physics separation and hand transfer. State fields store requests and bookkeeping; changing a field alone does not carry out the corresponding lock, body setup or grab-handler changes.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.AmmoGroup
member.summary: Defines a Unity asset that groups types under one shared ammunition count in .

remarks.para: An asset is saved project data that components can reference. This ScriptableObject, Unity's reusable data-asset type, contains a text key and a list of cartridge descriptions. The text key identifies the reserve entry, and the list tells the inventory which cartridge names use it. The changing amount is stored in AmmoInventory as a whole number of rounds, rather than in this asset.

The inventory registers its configured light, medium and heavy groups during Awake, Unity's initialization routine before normal component startup. Adding ammunition through a group can also register it. Registration caches cartridge-name-to-key mappings. A key already registered keeps its existing mappings, so changing the asset afterward does not automatically regroup the stored ammunition.

For example, two cartridge types registered under ExampleLight share a reserve: adding 20 rounds of one and 10 of the other increases that reserve by 30, and either type's count query reads it. Distinct keys keep counts separate. Reusing a key on another group shares the count but skips registering that other group's cartridge list.

Assign a non-null key, a non-null cartridge array and valid cartridge entries before registration. The initial key is empty text, which can unintentionally join several groups under the same key. Referencing or editing this asset alone does not add ammunition; additions and removals happen through the inventory.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.AmmoPlug
member.summary: A magazine-specific that updates inserted state and cartridge displays when seating or removal completes.

remarks.para: An alignment plug represents the part of an object that fits into a socket, such as a weapon's magazine opening. AlignPlug handles hand-guided alignment, socket locking, and insertion and removal transitions. This class adds completion callbacks, methods called by that alignment code when a transition finishes, for the assigned Magazine.

On insertion completion it sets the magazine's inserted flag before hiding its cartridge models. On removal completion it clears the flag before refreshing those models from the remaining ammunition count. A cartridge is a complete round of ammunition; the magazine can display its first two rounds when available. For example, with both targets and both art objects configured and live, removing a three-round magazine requests its first two displays active.

Assign the public magazine field during setup to the Magazine this plug represents. The inspected constructor and inherited Awake, Unity’s initialization callback for a Unity component, do not fill it automatically. The completion callbacks require that reference.

A consuming socket can report IsClearOnInsert as true. After the insertion-state and display changes, AmmoPlug then clears its alignment connection and requests the magazine's despawn, returning its pooled object to storage for reuse. The ordinary base Socket reports false; the older AmmoSocket bases the choice on a live internalMagazine configuration on its gun. Successful insertion can therefore lead to consuming the physical magazine instead of leaving it visible in the socket.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.AnimationRig
member.summary: Builds the avatar's moving body pose from the tracked rig, physical support, avatar proportions, and procedural spine and leg calculations.

remarks.para: In this context a rig is a set of transforms representing body joints. RigManager calls OnEarlyUpdate during its early-update pass. This rig normally follows manager.remapHeptaRig: it solves a standing body and feet, has a separate aligned-seated branch, and has a separate ActiveRagdoll branch. Its configured SLZ_Body supplies the stepping calculation.

The pelvis is the hip area at the base of the spine. The spine curves turn normalized body height into angular posture corrections. Movement supplies a smoothed lean direction, and controller grip changes the hand shape used for torso-proximity correction. A saved rotation pose briefly bridges OnFoot/ActiveRagdoll transitions. Most underscore fields are calculated history, so editing them is temporary; the configured curves, spineCrouchOffset, and suppression property have distinct input roles.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.ArtRig
member.summary: Transfers a simulated body’s movement to an avatar’s visible skeleton through calibrated helper transforms.

remarks.para: The physics rig provides the moving body frames. ArtRig keeps intermediate transforms for torso, limbs, hands, eyes and optional soft-body parts, then adds the model’s measured position and bone-axis corrections. The art-prefixed fields are these output helpers; the actual visible model bones are held by Avatar.artTransforms and its optional bone references.

MountRig attaches helpers to the appropriate physics frames, and SetArtOutputAvatar configures them for the selected avatar and its hand size. ArtOutputUpdate solves hand poses and intermediate wrist, gaze, shoulder-blade and soft-body motion. ArtOutputLateUpdate copies the resulting world poses to the active avatar’s bones. Optional twist output copies rotation only.

Assign the rig’s prepared helper hierarchy rather than substituting arbitrary visible bones into the helper fields. Manual edits to output bones can be replaced on the next update, and changing an Avatar measurement does not itself rerun mounting or calibration.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Atv
member.summary: Updates a quad bike's rear-wheel drive targets, wheel-contact sounds, and registered-driver motor audio and friction material.

remarks.para: Assign four wheel ConfigurableJoints, physics connections with configurable limits and motors, with a Rigidbody and Collider on each wheel object. A Rigidbody supplies mass and physical motion; a Collider supplies its contact shape. Also assign the chassis, axle, steering-wheel body, four contact sensors, driver seat, engine-sound component and collider used for the material swap.

Start, Unity's setup call before this component's first update, caches the four wheel bodies, configures their maximum angular velocity to 300 radians per second, and gives their colliders a 0.005-metre contact offset, the small separation at which physics prepares contacts. An assigned steering wheel receives a new joint connected to the axle; setup locks rotation about that joint's primary axis. This component's own Update does not convert grabbed steering-wheel angles into chassis steering torque.

Update is Unity's callback once per frame while this component is enabled. At its start, Update checks whether the mainBody chassis Rigidbody is sleeping. An awake update means it is not sleeping; Unity can put a nearly still Rigidbody to sleep to reduce physics work. A registered rider is the player's RigManager stored in driverSeat's Seat._rig reference; seat entry can register it before the rider is fully seated. Awake updates refresh the sensor results and weight contact and engine audio by a counted mass in kilograms. Its base is the sum of mainBody, frontAxle, steeringWheel, and the four cached wheel Rigidbody masses. The rider's stored avatar mass (RigManager._avatar._massTotal) is added only when driverSeat has a valid registered Seat._rig and that rig has a valid avatar reference. With no registered rider, the calculations use vehicle mass alone. A registered rider must have an avatar reference; if it is missing, this update fails before calculating the load. Awake updates use the registered rider's right-thumbstick input to request rear-wheel spin. With processed unitless throttle t from -1 to 1, configured maxSpeed v in metres per second, and wheelRadius r in metres, both rear joint targets have X spin -t * v / r radians per second and zero Y/Z components. Joint configuration and contacts determine actual motion; v is not a hard chassis-speed cap.

Seat registration, rather than a fully-seated test, starts and stops the _motorRunning engine-audio state and applies the corresponding physics material to the chosen collider. Engine modulation uses rear-left wheel spin relative to the chassis, not measured forward travel. One shared tire-sound loop follows the wheel with the greatest relative contact-point speed; it does not require a pavement surface. Sleeping chassis updates stop a playing tire loop and skip the other control/audio/material work, retaining their saved state until later awake updates.

Keep maxSpeed and wheelRadius positive because calculations divide by them, and provide all references expected by the awake update. Wheel-body and steering-joint setup is captured during Start; replacing wheel joints or axle references later does not rebuild those caches/connections. Sound fades and the engine's speed-change calculation use frame durations in scaled game-time seconds, so slow motion changes how they advance per real second.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Audio.AmbAndMusic
member.summary: Controls gradual volume changes for one ambience or music sound source.

remarks.para: This is a data helper rather than a Unity component that updates itself. Assign its ambMus AudioSource, the component that plays the sound, then start a fade and advance it once per frame with UpdateFade. Audio2dManager handles those updates for entries in its ambAndMusics array while their isFading flags are true.

FadeIn selects and starts a clip. AttenuateCurrent changes the volume of the source's existing clip, and FadeOut moves it toward silence and eventual stopping. Volume fades use real frame time, so slow motion does not lengthen them while updates continue.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Audio.Audio2dManager
member.summary: Manages background ambience, music transitions and changes to the mixer's room-like reverb.

remarks.para: Awake, Unity's initialization callback, creates three ambience sources and three music sources. They use 2D sound, so playback is not tied to distance from a world position. The extra sources allow old sounds to fade out while new sounds fade in.

Regular music cues can be remembered while a special override cue has control, then restored when override control is released. Source-volume fades use real frame time; reverb changes use game time and therefore respond to slow motion or pauses.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Audio.Audio2dPlugin
member.summary: Creates and exposes a persistent for background ambience and music before a level loads.

remarks.para: The level-loading system invokes this plugin's callback before a level loads. If the stored manager is missing or destroyed, the callback creates a GameObject, an object in the Unity scene, attaches the Audio2dManager script to it as a component, stores the manager reference, and marks its object to survive scene changes. A live manager is reused for later levels.

Adding the manager script invokes Awake, Unity's setup callback, which creates six AudioSource components (sound players). The plugin also starts loading an AudioMixer asset, which routes those players into ambience and music output groups when matching groups exist. Its level-load callback returns a completed task without waiting for this separate mixer load to finish.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Audio.Audio3dManager
member.summary: Starts asynchronous mixer-group loading and provides pooled playback helpers for world positions, parent-local positions, and 2D one-shot playback.

remarks.para: A Unity GameObject is a scene object that holds components. MonoBehaviour is Unity's base class for script components attached to GameObjects. An AudioMixer asset routes audio through named groups with their configured controls and effects; an AudioSource component plays an audio clip. Audio3dManager is a MonoBehaviour attached to a GameObject. When Unity loads a script component, it calls Awake, an initialization callback. A callback is a routine Unity calls at a defined point in that component's lifecycle. This method starts the asynchronous loader. When runtime settings and a mixer asset reference are available, it loads the configured mixer and caches group references, so getters can remain null until loading finishes. The master, music, and sound-effects properties store slider-style inputs and attempt writes to the corresponding exposed mixer parameters.

A sound-object pool is a set of reusable sound-player GameObjects. Playback helpers request one through an asynchronous spawn, which can reuse an available despawned sound-player object or load and instantiate its saved template. When spawning yields an object, the manager gets the AudioPlayer script component on it and calls Play, which configures and starts its AudioSource. The public helpers forget the asynchronous result, so returning only means the request started; it does not guarantee spawning succeeded or that a source has begun playing.

A Unity Transform is a component that stores an object's position, rotation, and scale; its local position is measured relative to its parent Transform. PlayAtPoint takes a world position in the scene coordinate frame. PlayAtLocalPoint takes a parent Transform and a local position relative to it. Here, “one-shot” means the AudioSource loop setting is false and one selected clip is played; the array overload randomly selects one clip when the array is nonempty. Play2dOneShot also sets spatial blend to zero, so that AudioSource uses 2D rather than 3D spatialization. A mixer group selects routing; the helper and spatial settings separately determine positional behavior.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Audio.Audio3dPlugin
member.summary: Requests registration of the reusable audio-player template and ensures a persistent exists on the normal level-load callback path when runtime settings are available and the audio-player Spawnable has a nonnull crate reference.

remarks.para: The configured audio-player Spawnable in runtime MarrowSettings, the game's active settings asset, holds two parts: a crate reference, which points to a content entry (a crate) in the game's asset warehouse by its barcode ID, and spawn-policy data. The level-load callback uses only the crate reference, to request registration of that crate's reusable sound-object template with the object pool, the system that supplies reusable sound objects. Registration does not read the spawn-policy data; that data is used later, when a spawn request passes this Spawnable to the spawner (for example, when the manager plays a sound at a position), to reuse or create the spawn policy that takes the object from the pool. The callback calls AssetSpawner.Register before manager handling. Register checks the crate reference before starting its separate registration work. If the reference is missing, registration fails immediately, so the callback does not continue to manager setup or return its usual completed task. On the normal path with a nonnull crate reference, the plugin creates a manager only when its saved reference is missing or destroyed; that manager's object survives scene changes. With a present reference, Register looks up the crate right away, before the callback continues to manager setup. If that lookup fails, no pool is added, but the callback continues to manager setup. If a matching pool already exists, Register does not add another; otherwise, it adds a new pool before manager setup. Only the new pool's template-prefab load can finish later without making the callback wait.

When runtime settings include a configured default-mixer reference, adding the manager starts LoadMixers. If runtime settings or that reference is absent, the loader returns without populating its channel groups; if the reference is configured but its AudioMixer is not loaded, the loader can load it asynchronously before caching those groups. This asynchronous setup does not delay the level-load callback's completed task. The callback requests template registration but does not wait for its prefab load; a manager reference or registration request is setup state, not proof that the template has finished loading or a requested sound has begun playing.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Audio.AudioPlayer
member.summary: Plays sounds through an assigned source on a reusable object and returns it to its pool after playback stops.

remarks.para: The pool is the system that reuses sound objects instead of creating a new one for every clip. Awake, Unity's initialization callback, registers this player in the object-to-component lookup and captures source settings. Pool initialization restores those settings, and deinitialization stops the sound, clears its clip and clears the playback-request flag.

Play chooses a clip and source settings; Attenuate changes volume, pitch and near-distance settings immediately. Update, Unity's per-frame callback, requests pool return when a Play request has set the flag and the source is no longer playing, provided the object is active and game timeScale is positive. The request flag does not prove that a clip successfully began.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Audio.FootstepSFX
member.summary: Plays individual positional footsteps from separate walking and running clip banks.

remarks.para: Awake, Unity's initialization callback, finds an AudioSource on the same object or adds one. An AudioSource is the component that plays sound clips. Setup disables automatic playback and the optional spatializer effect, sets fully positional 3D playback, selects Audio3dManager's current footsteps mixer group, and sets a minimum distance of 0.6 Unity world units (0.6 meters if the scene uses 1 unit = 1 meter). Distance is measured from this sound source to the listener; this minimum distance is the near-distance reference for the source's configured volume falloff, not a maximum hearing distance.

The mixer group, a channel controlling the sound's route through audio effects and volume controls, is assigned during that initialization. Changing the manager's group reference later does not by itself update this source. Each PlayStep call chooses a bank using the caller's movement value, replaces the current sound, and applies a new volume and pitch. Callers control the timing of steps; attaching this component alone does not create a footstep rhythm.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Audio.ManagedAudioPlayer
member.summary: Controls a reusable pooled at a world point or a point attached to another object.

remarks.para: The pool keeps sound objects available for reuse. This wrapper stores the latest clip and settings, reuses its existing player when the pool ID still matches, or starts an asynchronous spawn that can finish later. Further requests during that wait update the shared settings; they do not each create a separate pending player. A completed spawn requests playback with the then-current settings.

World playback uses scene coordinates in meters. Local playback attaches the sound object to a parent Transform, the object's position, rotation and scale, and uses that parent's axes and scale. One-shot calls request a single pass; loop calls request repetition and start at a random sample position. Stop clears the pending flag and stops only a matching player.

The editable properties work while a matching player or pending spawn exists; with neither, their setters ignore changes. Their getters return saved settings, while isPlaying queries a matching source or reports a pending request. Pending and configured state do not establish that sound is already audible.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Audio.MusicAmbience2dSFX
member.summary: Legacy component that crossfades nonpositional music and ambience, defers regular music during overrides, and changes mixer reverb.

remarks.para: This class is marked obsolete with a compiler error. Its replacement is Audio2dPlugin.Audio2dManager. These remarks describe the legacy class for existing content and inspection.

It uses two ambience sources and two music sources, letting an old clip fade out while a new clip fades in. Awake, Unity's initialization callback, prepares their AudioSources and 2D mixer routes. An AudioSource is the component that plays sound clips; 2D sound here does not pan or fade based on its position relative to the listener.

Volume fades, timed override release and reverb transitions use scaled game seconds. The intro-to-loop wait uses real-time seconds. Pausing or slowing the game can therefore affect these stages differently. Fade progress and coroutine checks occur on frames rather than exact wall-clock instants.

During override mode, regular music cues save the music to request on release. The overriden fields hold those deferred settings, not necessarily the currently audible override. Releasing the mode attempts restoration only when the required saved clips exist.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Audio.MusicAmbience2dSFX.AmbAndMusic
member.summary: Holds one sound source and the clip and volume-fade settings driven by .

remarks.para: The legacy parent uses entries 0 and 1 for ambience and entries 2 and 3 for music. Two sources allow the old clip to fade out while a new clip fades in. During Awake, Unity's initialization callback, the parent keeps an assigned AudioSource or adds one, prepares nonpositional 2D playback and assigns the appropriate mixer group. An AudioSource plays sound clips; a mixer group routes them through shared effects and volume controls.

FadeIn stops the old sound, stores and assigns the requested clip, prepares an immediate volume or a fade up from zero, and requests playback. FadeOut prepares a fade toward zero when the source is playing with positive volume and a positive duration; otherwise it stops and silences the source immediately. AttenuateCurrent changes the volume target for the existing clip and can restart a stopped source when that target is positive.

The clip field is the reference saved by FadeIn, not a getter for the live source's current clip. The fade fields are stored settings: isFading asks the parent's Update to run a fade step, fadeTarget is a unitless source-volume target, and fadePerSec is volume change per scaled game second. Directly editing them does not change the source until a fade step applies them. Not every setup path clamps the target, so ordinary targets from 0 through 1 and nonnegative fade rates are appropriate.
This entry belongs to the obsolete MusicAmbience2dSFX system, whose replacement is Audio2dPlugin.Audio2dManager. Its volume fades use scaled game time, so they pause and slow with game time scale.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.AvatarGrip
member.summary: Lets a hand grab a point on an avatar's physical body and aligns the hand target with that body surface.

remarks.para: The hand target is the desired position and rotation the game asks the physical hand to reach.

The component uses _physRig for torso colliders and avatar body measurements. bodyRb chooses the body-region search. Rather than using one fixed grab position, it calculates a contact for each hand and remembers that contact for hover and attachment updates.

For chest, spine, and pelvis contacts, the hover target follows the avatar's shaped torso surface. Joint-configuration updates then adjust the hand's rotational limits and spring settings. A joint is the physics connection that keeps the hand attached to the grabbed object. Its rotational spring setting controls how strongly that connection tries to restore the intended rotation.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.BallisticPassthrough
member.summary: Lets Projectile skip selected collider hits before ordinary attack and impact processing, using an optional directional rule.

remarks.para: Projectile searches along its travel using a raycast, a straight-line check for invisible physics shapes called colliders. When it hits a shape, it looks for BallisticPassthrough on that collider’s own GameObject, the Unity scene object carrying the shape. A component only on a parent or another object is not found by this lookup.

With isPassthrough true, the test permits skipping regardless of the struck face’s orientation. With false, it still permits skipping when the hit’s surface normal, the direction perpendicular to the struck face, points partly along the component object’s forward positive Z axis. The comparison uses directions in the whole scene’s axes and requires a positive dot product; an exactly sideways or opposite face fails. Rotate the object to change which directions qualify. Normal reports this object’s current forward direction, rather than the latest face normal.

For an accepted skip, the projectile moves to the hit point and searches farther along its existing travel direction. The next search begins 0.001 meters, about one millimeter, beyond the face in the direction opposite its outward normal. That skipped hit bypasses the ordinary attack dispatch and penetration-resistance branch; a later hit can still be processed normally.

The passthrough loop skips at most four hits during one Projectile update, a routine run for one step of the game’s ongoing work. A further hit found after that reaches ordinary handling. This component does not remove or disable its collider, so it does not make the object intangible to the player or other physics objects. The inspected projectile routine reads the component without testing its script-enabled setting; changing isPassthrough or its orientation controls the rule described here.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.BarrelGrip
member.summary: Chooses a hand pose and target for grabbing a barrel’s side, uncapped rim, capped end, or a very short shape held across its ends.

remarks.para: The capsule collider supplies the geometric frame and dimensions. Zone checks consider where the hand is, how it faces the surface, the enabled cap flags, padding, and allowed distance from the proposed handle. A valid result is cached for that hand and used during hover and attachment.

Use ringHandPose, sideHandPose, edgeHandPose, and capHandPose to set the region-specific finger poses. heightAndRadiusCurve can override the checked span and side radius profile. The region-specific break-force fields are stored in the hand cache, but the audited barrel updater does not apply them as live joint-break thresholds.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.BaseController
member.summary: Represents one VR hand controller with shared input storage and virtual methods for controller-specific behavior.

remarks.para: This API covers interaction buttons, face and menu buttons, thumbstick and touchpad input, finger curl, grip timing and vibration feedback. A controller subclass can replace a virtual method, meaning it supplies its own behavior when that method is called. OpenController is an input-specific implementation; the plain BaseController does not poll a device in its empty OnUpdate hook.

The base interaction and finger getters read saved values. Many other base button/touch methods return false, the base grip-velocity getter returns 0, and its world-velocity getter returns (0, 0, 0). Its base touchpad-axis getter reads the thumbstick vector. These defaults do not prove what a connected physical controller is doing.

Finger and pull amounts normally use the unitless range 0 for open/released to 1 for fully curled/pulled. Thumbstick vectors use controller input directions rather than scene positions. The five processed finger values start at 0.2 in the constructor. Input-specific updates or StampController can supply later cached values; a read itself does not consume them.

Grab transition flags, grab threshold conditions and recent-grab timing answer different questions. They describe grip input rather than an actual held scene object. Recent-grab timestamps use unscaled game-clock seconds, unaffected by slow motion. Movement velocity supplied by supporting controllers is metres per second on world axes relative to head movement; the base returns zero.

Assign handedness, the controller rig reference and any Haptor vibration component for the chosen implementation’s setup. A rig groups the player’s head and hands; a Haptor prepares vibration effects. The base vibration hooks are empty even when that component is assigned, so device behavior comes from the controller implementation.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Blueprints.BillOfMaterials
member.summary: Provides named Unity component references that blueprint restoration can look up when rebuilding signal connections.

remarks.para: A blueprint is saved setup describing objects to spawn and connections to restore. This component supplies a dictionary, a collection pairing text keys with Unity component references. A Unity component is a part attached to an object, such as code that sends or receives a switch signal.

The resolver looks up a key in the supplied Components collection and returns the registered reference. For example, a blueprint can use "doorSwitch" to find a registered switch component on a spawned object. VoidLogic connection restoration uses these lookups to obtain signal sources and receivers before rebuilding their connections.

Components and AllComponents expose the same live collection. Reading them does not discover or create components. The collection must be provided by saved setup or setup code before resolution; the constructor only performs the base Unity component initialization. A key absent from an existing collection returns null and takes the resolver’s diagnostic path. Merely editing the collection does not spawn the blueprint or run connection restoration.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Blueprints.Blueprint
member.summary: A holding a recipe for creating a group of objects and restoring their VoidLogic signal wires.

remarks.para: This is a data asset, rather than the created objects themselves. Assign it to a BlueprintSpawner, the scene component that reads the recipe when asked to spawn. Each spawn record identifies an object asset and gives a position offset in Unity scene units plus an orientation relative to the spawner. VoidLogic carries signals between components, which are behaviors attached to spawned objects; each wire connects one component’s output to another’s input. The connection data records those wires within the group.

For example, a recipe can describe a button and a door, their spacing, and the wire connecting the button’s output to the door’s input. Provide the spawn array, valid crate references, and an edges array for the wires; use an empty edges array if no wiring is needed.

The spawner creates an inactive parent at its own position and orientation, requests the recipe’s objects, waits for creation to complete, then restores the wires. It activates the parent after restoration succeeds. An asynchronous request can still be waiting for objects, so the existence of this card or the start of a spawn call does not prove that a usable group has been created.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Blueprints.BlueprintSpawner
member.summary: Prepares a blueprint’s assets and creates copies of its saved object layout and signal connections.

remarks.para: A blueprint stores which objects to create, their relative positions and rotations, and their logic wiring, the connections that let objects send signals to one another. Awake, Unity’s component initialization callback (a routine called to initialize the component), starts preparing the assets. It does not automatically create the object group.

SpawnBlueprint and SpawnBlueprintAsync create a fresh parent at the spawner’s world position and rotation, place the saved objects under it, and restore their wiring before activating the parent. Saved position offsets are meters. Their orientation follows the spawner’s rotation; this path does not scale those offsets by the spawner’s scale. Asset spawning can wait and continue in later frames.

ShouldSpawn is an optional callback, a routine asked whether the request may proceed. It is checked once before object creation unless ignoreCondition is true. A false result prevents that request; it does not prevent initialization from preparing assets. Keep the Blueprint reference stable while a request is waiting, because the restoration stage reads it again.

Repeated allowed requests create separate groups in the inspected path. A reported missing crate reference, unresolved crate or unsuccessful wiring restoration destroys that request’s new parent instead of activating it. Reset and ResetName rename the spawner’s own object; they do not clear the blueprint assignment or despawn earlier groups.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Blueprints.BlueprintVLSerializing
member.summary: Writes the saved descriptions of VoidLogic signal wires into JSON objects. The ReadJson overloads have native limitations and do not restore the supplied records.

remarks.para: A VoidLogic connection describes wires for gameplay signals, such as connecting a button output to a device input. Each edge is one wire: from identifies its output endpoint and to identifies its input endpoint.

JSON stores named values and lists as text-friendly data. Here a connection writes an edges array, each edge writes from and to objects, and each endpoint writes spawnableIndex, spawnableKey and portIndex.

Each endpoint writes spawnableIndex, spawnableKey and portIndex. spawnableIndex is the zero-based position of the spawned object in the blueprint spawn list; 0 means the first object. spawnableKey is the text key used to find the signal component in that object’s bill of materials, its list of named parts. portIndex selects the numbered output on from or input on to; these indices are unitless counts, not distances or signal strengths.
Only these three endpoint fields are written. useInlinePower and inlinePowerValue are not included by this writer; do not assume this JSON preserves those additional port settings.

The writers fill the supplied JObject, the editable JSON object, immediately; they do not spawn objects or connect live signal components. Restoring actual connections is a separate VoidLogicConnection.Restore operation after the blueprint objects exist.

The read overloads take their record by value, meaning a temporary copy, and return no updated record. In addition, the connection reader expects edges to be a JObject rather than the JArray produced by the writer; the port reader looks for handle rather than spawnableKey and converts portIndex without storing it. Use your own explicit parsing and assignments if you need a reliable save/load round trip.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Blueprints.IConnection
member.summary: Common interface for restoring saved links to objects created from a blueprint.

remarks.para: A blueprint is a saved recipe describing objects to create and links between them. An interface is a common form that different implementations follow. IConnection defines Restore: the implementation receives the BlueprintSpawner managing the spawn, an array pairing each SpawnData recipe entry with its spawned Poolee, the object’s component for reuse by the game, and bomCache, a lookup of each object’s IBillOfMaterials, its list of named components.

The game’s VoidLogicConnection implementation uses those spawned-object entries and named components to find a signal source and receiving input, then asks the receiving node to reconnect each saved link. For example, a saved button output linked to a lamp input can be restored to the newly created button and lamp, instead of retaining references to the original scene objects. The cache avoids repeatedly finding an object’s named-component lookup during this pass.

The blueprint spawner waits for its object-spawn operations to finish before this restoration pass. Restore itself returns a Boolean rather than a task to wait for. The supplied implementation reports false for lookup failures such as missing objects or named source/receiver components, and true after processing its saved links. It does not check the Boolean returned by each receiving node’s connection call, so true is not a guarantee that every receiving input accepted the link. A node can also queue its graph update for later processing.

The inspected BlueprintSpawner calls its stored VoidLogicConnection directly. Merely implementing IConnection on a custom type does not make that spawner discover or invoke it. This interface defines a restoration operation; it does not create the blueprint’s objects itself or specify a rendered-frame delay for applying their links.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Blueprints.SpawnData
member.summary: Stores one blueprint entry’s spawnable asset selection and its placement relative to the spawner.

remarks.para: Blueprint.spawnables is a list of these saved entries. crateRef identifies a spawnable crate, the asset description for the object to create. transform stores the entry’s position offset and rotation. It contains position and orientation only, without scale. This record is a recipe for one object; storing or copying it does not itself create a scene object.

When BlueprintSpawner spawns the list, it checks each crate reference and passes the entry to its spawn operation. The position offset uses meters along the spawner’s right, up and forward axes. The saved rotation is a quaternion, Unity’s four-number orientation representation, relative to the spawner’s rotation. The spawner rotates each offset and adds its own position to obtain the scene position, measured in the whole level’s axes. Thus a saved offset of (2, 0, 0) places the object two meters to the spawner’s right, even when the spawner has turned.

SpawnData is a value type: copying it copies its position and rotation values along with the reference to the selected crate. The crate reference still identifies the same asset; the copy does not make a new asset. BlueprintSpawner copies the record into a spawn request and, on success, pairs it with the resulting object. Editing a saved entry afterward does not retarget or move that existing object through the inspected spawn routines.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.BodyPose
member.summary: Stores a body-pose sample that rigs can copy, blend and adapt to an avatar's proportions.

remarks.para: A pose is saved data about where the body is aiming and reaching: segment orientations, arm and leg reach fractions, palm proximity to the other hand and torso, scaled root and head positions, and a timestamp. A rig is the set of reference transforms and bones that captures or applies those values. Editing this object changes data; a rig must apply that data to move the body.

Many lengths are divided by an avatar measurement so the pose can be adapted to another body size. Arm and leg extensions and hand proximity are unitless ratios. Controller-captured root and head positions use skull-height units, meaning one unit is the avatar's stored skull-height reference length in metres. The timestamp is game time in seconds. Each position and direction also has its own reference axes; root, chest, rig-object and palm axes can differ.

Rotations are quaternions, which store orientations as four numbers rather than angles in degrees. A new pose starts with identity rotations, meaning no added turn; both head-position vectors start at (0, 1, 0). Fill a pose from the rig or set its values before treating those defaults as a measured body sample.

For example, copy a current pose into a separate BodyPose to keep a sample, then blend two compatible samples with a unitless factor. CopyPose includes timestamp, while AddPose and LerpPoseUnclamped leave the destination timestamp unchanged. Blending does not by itself capture, apply or time a new pose.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.BoxGrip
member.summary: Lets each hand grab an oriented box at a face, edge, corner or sufficiently thin section with a matching pose.

remarks.para: Assign _boxCollider to define the shape. The enabled face, edge and corner masks choose allowed regions, and the mode permission switches enable the kinds of grab. edgePadding divides surface regions; sandwichSize identifies thin dimensions for a hand wrapping across opposing sides.

Contact validation selects geometry for each hand and stores its local target plus a separate HandPose/radius entry. Hover turns the saved target into a world-space pose, and attached-hand updates retain the selected animation. Joint configuration controls the physical rotational connection holding the hand to the object.

Force pulling uses a separately configured alignment from forceGrabFace and forceGrabTop, with sandwichHandPose. A sandwich grab is a single-hand mode; this component does not require a two-hand squeeze to use it.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.BoxGrip.Corners
member.summary: Selects which of a box grip’s eight corner regions can be used for corner grabs.

remarks.para: Assign these flags to BoxGrip.enabledCorners. Each value represents one corner relative to the referenced BoxCollider’s center and rotated axes: X is right/left, Y is up/down and Z is forward/back. Positive and negative signs choose the corresponding side of each axis. The axes turn with the box; they are not fixed world directions.

Combine flags with the bitwise OR operator (|) to allow multiple corners. For example, PositiveXPositiveYPositiveZ | NegativeXPositiveYPositiveZ enables both upper, forward corners. A value of 0 selects no corners; the combination of all eight values is 255.

BoxGrip.CheckZones checks the selected corner bit and canBeCornerGrabbed before preparing a corner grab. The selected hand pose affects the hand’s alignment. cornerHandPoseRadius is an offset distance in metres: a positive value moves the grab point inward from the chosen corner along a diagonal with equal X, Y and Z parts. Enabling a corner does not require the hand to sit exactly on its mathematical vertex. Faces, edges and sandwich grabs have separate settings.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.BoxGrip.Edges
member.summary: Flags selecting which of a box’s twelve edges are eligible for edge-style hand grabs.

remarks.para: Assign these flags to BoxGrip.enabledEdges. Combine values with the bitwise OR operator, |, to allow several edges. For example, PositiveXPositiveY | NegativeXPositiveY selects the two Z-running edges where the positive-Y face meets either X face. A zero mask selects no edges for this grab mode.

The two named axes identify the faces that meet; the unnamed third axis runs along the edge. Signs and axes follow the box collider’s orientation relative to its center, so rotating the box rotates the selected edges in the world.

BoxGrip.canBeEdgeGrabbed must also be true. Selected edges still have to pass the hand-position and orientation checks. An accepted edge grab uses edgeHandPose, the saved hand-and-finger pose, and edgeHandPoseRadius, the radius in metres used to place the hand and choose its curl around the edge. Face, corner, and sandwich grabs have separate settings, so clearing an edge flag does not by itself forbid every way to hold the nearby area.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.BoxGrip.Faces
member.summary: Identifies the box’s six local faces for grab filtering and force-pull hand orientation.

remarks.para: For enabledFaces, combine values with | to allow more than one face. For example, PositiveX | NegativeX allows the two opposite X faces. Face-style grabs also require canBeFaceGrabbed and must pass the hand-position and orientation checks. Accepted face grabs use faceHandPose, the saved hand-and-finger pose, and faceHandPoseRadius, the radius in metres passed to the finger-fit solver for that face grab. The face mask is also checked when deciding whether a thin box can be held across its sides.

For forceGrabFace or forceGrabTop, choose one face per field: these settings are converted into a single direction for the force-pull hand target. Combined flags do not produce a diagonal direction; the conversion returns a zero vector for an unrecognized combination. Use two perpendicular face directions to describe the target’s orientation clearly.

Axis signs follow the box collider’s orientation relative to its center. PositiveX is toward local red X, PositiveY toward local green Y, and PositiveZ toward local blue Z; negative values choose the opposite sides. Rotating the box rotates those sides in the world. A face direction is not a distance or speed.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.CameraSettings
member.summary: Enables dithering, post-processing and the invalid-number filter in the attached camera's Universal Render Pipeline settings during initialization.

remarks.para: Universal Render Pipeline, or URP, is Unity's system for drawing the scene. Put this component on the same scene object as a Camera, which supplies the view, and UniversalAdditionalCameraData, which holds the camera's extra rendering options. A component is a part attached to a scene object. The Camera requirement does not add the separate URP data component.

Awake is the routine Unity calls when initializing the component. It saves the two component references, then sets dithering, renderPostProcessing, and stopNaN to true on the saved URP data object and logs a message. These are true/false switches. Dithering uses a small noise pattern to reduce visible color bands; post-processing allows image effects after the scene is drawn; stopNaN requests filtering of invalid numeric pixel values, where NaN means “not a number.”

The renderer reads those switches while preparing its rendering data. This setup configures later drawing; it does not itself draw a frame, meaning one image produced by the game, or guarantee that every requested effect runs. The active rendering path, image-effect settings and graphics support still matter. A missing URP data component makes initialization fail when the switches are written.

For example, attach CameraSettings and the URP data component to a camera before it initializes to request all three switches. Editing one of the cached references afterward only changes that reference; it does not rerun initialization or automatically configure a different camera. The two references are found together during setup, so keep them matched when changing them yourself.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Circuits.Actuator
member.summary: Base component for turning numeric signals from objects into actions.

remarks.para: A circuit calculates a number; an actuator's derived Actuate routine decides what to do with its input numbers. The base Actuate routine does nothing. SetupInputs chooses the connections, Initialize prepares the actuator, and a later initial evaluation calls Actuate with initialization enabled.

During a normal RecursiveUpdate, older input circuits are refreshed before the action runs. Circuit propagation reaches connected actuators when a circuit's calculated output changes; the base actuator does not provide its own every-frame update loop. An assigned ExternalActuator can instead forward its evaluations through a callback, meaning a connected routine called by the companion.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Circuits.AddCircuit
member.summary: Adds the calculated output numbers of its configured inputs.

remarks.para: The calculation starts at 0 and adds every entry in array order. Outputs 2 and -0.5 produce 1.5; duplicate entries contribute repeatedly, and an empty input array produces 0. The result is not limited to 0 through 1. The signals determine the units, so connect quantities that make sense to add together.

The result becomes inlineValue, the node's calculated output, during circuit evaluation. Setting up or assigning inputs rebuilds connections without immediately calculating the result. Input entries must be valid circuits; missing entries are not safely replaced or ignored by this node.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Circuits.ButtonController
member.summary: Converts a physical button's joint travel into a circuit signal according to , with sound requests on recognized presses and releases.

remarks.para: The Servo measures signed displacement along the joint's X direction in meters; the controller turns this into an adjusted reading from 0 to 1 across the current allowed travel. A joint is the physics connection limiting the button's motion. Click modes produce pulses, Toggle remembers on/off state and changes the joint's travel, ContinuousDown reports a held press, and ContinuousFloat reports the travel reading itself.

The inherited physics-step update reads the button while its Rigidbody is awake and its joint exists. A Rigidbody is Unity's component for an object moved by the physics simulation; awake means it is actively simulated rather than sleeping at rest. The result is a sensor value, and a connected CircuitSocket input can multiply it before the final circuit output is published.

Initialization samples the starting position and latches without requesting transition sounds. Later recognized press/release transitions update their latch before requesting one randomly selected sound at the component's world position. ContinuousFloat skips those sounds. Reading a click pulse again normally clears it, so a pulse does not have a guaranteed duration in rendered frames.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Circuits.ButtonController.ButtonMode
member.summary: Chooses how a turns its physical travel into a sensor number: click pulses, a toggle, a held state, or continuous travel.

remarks.para: The threshold modes press above an adjusted reading of 0.9 and release below 0.1. Readings between those boundaries keep their stored state. The reading spans the current joint's travel from 0 to 1 after a 1.04 multiplier, 0.02 subtraction and limiting to that range. Toggle changes the joint's allowed travel; ContinuousFloat bypasses the thresholds and transition sounds.

Selecting another mode does not clear the stored press state or Toggle on/off and rearm state, and does not restore joint settings changed by Toggle. The mode determines sensorValue; a connected CircuitSocket input can multiply that number to produce inlineValue, the final calculated circuit output. Click pulses depend on when the sensor is read, rather than a fixed duration in frames or seconds.

Button displacement is measured in meters along the Servo’s configured joint-X direction; the joint is the physics connection controlling that travel. CircuitSocket samples each mode during Unity FixedUpdate only while its Rigidbody (physics-body component) is awake and the Servo has a live joint. The physics timestamp is Time.fixedTime in seconds; a sleeping body or missing joint pauses later reads.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Circuits.CircuitSocket
member.summary: Base circuit for physical sensors that uses a joint and a , with an optional input multiplier.

remarks.para: A physics joint controls movement between physical objects; a Rigidbody lets Unity's physics simulation move an object. The automatic FixedUpdate, Unity's routine called on physics steps, checks whether the stored body is awake and the Servo's joint exists before requesting circuit evaluation at Unity Time.fixedTime, the time at the start of the current FixedUpdate, measured in seconds since the game started. Reset can fill missing references from this object or its children.

Derived classes supply the physical sensor reading. The socket's InlineCalculate multiplies that reading by the first connected input's calculated output, or passes it through when no input exists. The base socket does not convert a signal number into a target orientation or apply a joint drive in this update routine.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Circuits.ExternalCircuit
member.summary: Evaluates circuit signals through optional initialization, sensor-reading and output-calculation callbacks.

remarks.para: A callback is a routine called to obtain or process a value. Without assigned routines, initialization returns sensor number 0, later sensor reads retain the previous number, and calculation multiplies that sensor by the configured source's output or passes it through when no source exists.

Another Circuit can use this object as an externalCircuit companion, installing its own routines while this object stores the active sensor, output and timestamp caches. Those routine assignments can replace callbacks you installed earlier, and network initialization can run more than once.

Input setup resolves a configured source's companion for wiring; fallback multiplication directly reads the configured source's own calculated-output cache. Signals have the units and ranges chosen by their routines, with no universal 0-to-1 range or unit conversion supplied by this class.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Circuits.ExternalCircuit.InitializeDelegate
member.summary: A routine assigned to to supply the starting sensor number.

remarks.para: This callback, meaning a routine the circuit calls to obtain a value, takes no arguments and returns a float. Its units and range depend on the sensor you implement. During Circuit.InitializingUpdate, the returned float is stored as sensorValue. That value is passed to InlineCalculate; its separate return is stored as inlineValue before initialization continues. Calling the delegate directly runs its assigned method and returns a float, but does not by itself perform those Circuit.InitializingUpdate cache writes or continue network initialization.

Initialization can run again after startup. Another Circuit using the ExternalCircuit as its companion can replace this routine with the owning Circuit’s Initialize method during setup or companion assignment.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Circuits.ExternalCircuit.InlineCalculateDelegate
member.summary: A routine assigned to to turn a sensor number into the circuit's calculated output.

remarks.para: This callback, meaning a routine called to process a value, receives a float sensorValue and returns a float output. sensorValue is the sampled sensor number; the return becomes inlineValue, the calculated output other circuits can read. Units and range depend on your sensor and calculation. For example, a routine that doubles an input of 0.25 returns 0.5.

An assigned routine replaces ExternalCircuit's fallback input multiplication. Its caller stores and propagates the returned output under the circuit's evaluation rules; invoking the delegate directly only returns a number. Another Circuit using the ExternalCircuit as its companion can replace this routine with its own InlineCalculate hook during setup or companion assignment.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Circuits.ValueCircuit
member.summary: Supplies a configurable constant number to a circuit network.

remarks.para: Initialize and ReadSensor both return the configured _value, and InlineCalculate passes it through unchanged. The number has no built-in physical units or 0-to-1 limit: for example, 0.5 can be a multiplier when connected to a node that treats it that way.

Assigning Value stores the new configuration and requests an update, but the normal current-physics-time guard can leave the published output older until a later eligible evaluation. Directly writing _value only changes configuration. The constructor begins at 1; serialized object settings can differ.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.CollisionCollector
member.summary: Collects contact impulses and reports a reusable collision payload through enter and stay callbacks.

remarks.para: This Unity component, behaviour attached to a scene object, gathers collision information for physical effects. Its OnCollisionEnter accepts contacts only when the other object has ImpactProperties, material/impact information. The companion CollisionStay similarly forwards continuing contacts when that information is present. During editor Reset setup, each component finds its partner on the same object.

The collector adds nonzero impulse vectors, pushes delivered over time in newton seconds, and keeps the details of the individual collision with the largest impulse. Coordinates use world space, the level's shared axes. Contact positions and separation use metres; relative velocity uses metres per second. Equal-strength contacts keep the earlier details.

The owning body's update code calls ProcessCollisionHaul to report results. A callback is a method called with that result. The enter branch tests signed speed along the selected contact normal; the stay branch does not. The payload is reused and its totalImpulse and rigidbody, the other physically simulated body component, are cleared after reporting. The retained stay flag can cause another report without a new contact.

The two-argument processing method also saves a scaled impulse after the callback returns. Its caller chooses the scale and therefore the units; PhysicsRig, the component that simulates the player's physical body, uses a fraction of body weight. The one-argument method leaves that pressure value unchanged. Register listeners and configure both components before expecting reports.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.CollisionCollector.RelevantCollision
member.summary: Collision data collected by , combining an accumulated impulse with details from one selected collision report.

remarks.para: The collector adds the impulse vectors from accepted collision reports. An impulse is a push accumulated over time, measured in newton-seconds when distance and mass use metres and kilograms. The collider references, surface settings, relative linear velocity and contact details come from the report with the largest impulse magnitude, meaning the size of that report's push. A report of equal strength keeps the earlier details. Point, normal and separation are copied from the first contact of that selected report.

For example, after any direction correction, a report contributing (2, 0, 0) and a later report contributing (0, 3, 0) produce a total of (2, 3, 0) newton-seconds. The contact details describe the second report, even though the total includes both. The vectors and positions use the scene's world axes, rather than the object's rotated local axes.

The ordinary collision-enter and collision-stay callbacks, functions Unity calls when contact begins or continues, only submit reports for which their cached lookup finds a live ImpactProperties surface-settings component on the other collision object. A direct CollectCollision call can supply different data. Reports with zero squared impulse magnitude do not update the stored collision values.

This is a mutable record that the collector creates once and reuses. Its reporting callbacks receive that same object. Normal processing clears totalImpulse and sets rigidbody, the other object's physics body component, to null after the callbacks return, while leaving the remaining contact values stored. Copy the values you need inside the callback to keep a record of an event; saving only the object reference does not make a snapshot.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Combat.Attack
member.summary: A damage-and-impact message containing an amount, position, orientation, category, hit shape and source identity.

remarks.para: Attack is a struct, a bundle of values normally copied when passed to ReceiveAttack. It does not perform a hit test, move a projectile or subtract health by itself. The sender supplies the data and separately chooses the scene object whose attack-receiving components should receive it. A receiver can apply damage, request an effect, or ignore the message according to its own rules.

For a simple impact, damage = 10 is ten game damage units, origin = (2, 1, 3) is the impact point in level coordinates, normal = (0, 1, 0) is the upward arrow perpendicular to the surface, and direction = (0, -1, 0) is a downward trajectory arrow. World positions use Unity world length units, meters at the usual meter scale; these orientation arrows are not positions or speeds. attackType identifies the category, collider is the invisible hit-test shape, and proxy can identify the initiating character. These values describe the requested attack, not its final health or physics result.

The inspected producers usually send world positions and directions, but receivers can convert copies into their own local coordinates. For example, PlayerDamageReceiver converts the point and surface normal into the receiving body part's frame before forwarding them. ImpactProperties copies the message before starting effects that can wait for assets to load, so later changes to your original bundle do not rewrite that copied request.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Combat.IAttackReceiver
member.summary: Provides the common attack-response entry point that Unity's event system calls through .

remarks.para: An interface is a contract: it gives different components the same method that an attack sender can call. Unity's event system delivers an attack to matching receiver components on the object chosen by the sender. A callback is the function used during this delivery to call ReceiveAttack with the attack record.

The contract does not choose one response for every object. AttackReceiver raises an event, GenericAttackReceiver filters attack types before raising a damage-valued event, and MuscleCollisionBroadcaster forwards the attack and the struck body-part index to its puppet behaviors. A puppet is the collection of physics-controlled body parts making up that character.

For example, an attack-sensitive switch can react through an event without having character health. A character body part can forward the same kind of attack record to its puppet behavior. The sender chooses where to deliver the record, and the receiving implementation chooses the effect.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Combat.VisualDamageController
member.summary: Records visual hit matrices, prepares a cut cache, and applies the hit data to the materials of its configured renderers.

remarks.para: A matrix is a table of numbers encoding an effect's position, orientation and shape. VisualDamageReceiver supplies hit and cut matrices from attack or cut-region setup. The impact manager stores up to 32 hits using wrapping replacement, while CutPoint normally stores up to eight cuts with a separate replacement index. A cut region can be described by an ellipsoid, a stretched sphere.

Additions call UpdateArray, which first records the cut-list size and copies its matrices into CutPos. It then sends the impact manager's full hit array and active count to every selected renderer material. A shader is the material's drawing program; it must support those properties to show the hit effect. This refresh does not upload the cut cache, so recorded cuts and visible cuts are distinct.

Awake, Unity's initialization callback, prepares the controller's shader keys. OnEnable uses ResetHits, clearing the active hit count/write position and source cut list before refreshing the materials. A callback is a routine called to perform or report an action. Reset does not erase every cached matrix or reset the cut replacement index. collectSkins is a separate operation that replaces the renderer selection with skinned meshes, meshes animated by bones, on this object and active children.

For example, an accepted hit can add a mark matrix to the manager and refresh an NPC's configured skin materials. A later enable/reset refresh sends zero active hits. This component manages visual data; its stored counters are not NPC health. Changes to meshScaleFactor and hitScaleFactor affect hit matrices created by later attacks; the cut-matrix path is separate. Assigning references or editing a cache does not automatically rebuild or upload all dependent data.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Console.TokenParseContext
member.summary: Carries the candidate commands and caller-supplied type expectations for console conversion, plus a threshold for partial command-name suggestions.

remarks.para: A token is a piece of text the console is interpreting, such as the command name. The context supplies a set of eligible command wrappers, each pairing a command object with its declared names. Command-name conversion searches that set, and suggestions use the same set. The expected-type array records the caller’s type expectations; the context itself does not convert text or execute commands.

A newly constructed context has an empty command set and keeps the supplied expected-type array by reference. The built-in console plugin creates a context with an empty type array and a suggestion threshold of 20 when it loads, then fills the command set during command scans. For example, a context containing only a help-command wrapper restricts command-name matching to the names declared on that wrapper.

The suggestion threshold is measured in match entries. Exact aliases are checked before the threshold gate, so exact entries can exceed it when encountered first in a wrapper's alias list. Once the count reaches the threshold, the first non-exact alias ends that wrapper's remaining alias scan, so a later exact alias on that wrapper can be skipped. Exact and partial entries already added share the same counter. The command set and the contents of the expected-type array remain changeable even though their field references are declared readonly.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Constrainer
member.summary: Controls a held tool that selects object endpoints and prepares physics connections or removes its tracked connections.

remarks.para: A physics joint is a connection that limits how simulated bodies move. The tool connects through triggerGrip, the handle a hand attaches to, and responds to input through registered callbacks, functions run when its hand events occur.

Trigger-down casts from firePoint to record the first endpoint. While held after a valid first hit, a second raycast, a straight-line collision check, casts from firePoint2 and updates the second point. Both casts use maxRange meters and layerMask. Release uses the saved endpoint data with the current mode; it does not perform a new second cast.

Movable endpoints use MarrowBody, the game’s physics-body component, and positions relative to that body’s transform. A Transform stores position, rotation, and scale. Endpoints without a Marrow body use fixed world positions. Creation requires at least one Marrow body and rejects two endpoints on the same body. The Marrow joint builds its underlying Unity connection when its participating bodies are active and enabled.

Creation also makes attachment markers, a drawn line, and ConstraintTracker components that remember the connection. The line follows those markers as bodies move. Remove mode selects one of these trackers on the first selected object and requests destruction of its joint and visual tracking objects; it does not remove every joint on that object. Unity completes destruction through its normal cleanup timing.

The two laser objects and icon show the input phase and mode. They do not prove that a hit is current. A missed first cast blocks the usual held/release actions, while a missed second cast leaves older second-endpoint data stored. Merely changing a saved endpoint, mode, material, or force setting does not rebuild a connection already created.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Constrainer.ConstraintMode
member.summary: Chooses the connection that the tool creates, or selects removal of an existing connection.

remarks.para: An enum is a named set of choices. These choices are Tether (0), Weld (1), BallSocket (2), Elastic (3), EntangleRotation (4), EntagleVelocity (5), and Remove (6). They are individual modes, not flags to combine. The spelling EntagleVelocity is the actual name to use in code.

For the six creation modes, the tool records a first hit when pressed, updates the second hit while held, and creates a joint when released with usable endpoints. A joint is a connection that the physics simulation enforces between objects. At least one endpoint must be a movable MarrowBody, the game component representing a physical body; two endpoints on the same body do not create a connection. An endpoint without a movable body is treated as a fixed world attachment. Remove instead deletes one tracked connection on the first hit object.

For each hit, the tool uses the impact point where the physics ray hits the collider, the shape tested by that ray. If that hit has a movable MarrowBody, the tool converts the impact point to local coordinates, meaning coordinates relative to that body. Without a movable body, the point stays in world coordinates, the shared scene coordinates. The tool records the first point on press and refreshes the second point while held. Unity world positions use Unity world units, normally metres.

Changing the selected mode chooses the behavior for a later tool operation; it does not retune connections the tool has already created. The chosen creation mode produces stored joint settings, and the actual physics joint is built when its bodies are active and enabled. Distance limits and mass-based strengths are captured during creation. For example, choose Weld for a handle that must stay attached to a crate, or BallSocket for a prop that should swing around one pivot.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.ConstraintTracker
member.summary: Maintains the visual endpoints and cleanup for a connection created by the Constrainer tool.

remarks.para: A physics joint connects objects and restricts or drives their movement. The Constrainer creates that joint, two separate attachment markers and one visual line, then places a ConstraintTracker component on each selected object. The trackers refer to the same joint and line and point at each other; the markers supply the line’s moving world positions.

One tracker is marked isHost for automatic line refresh. During Unity’s per-frame Update routine, a missing or destroyed joint first triggers deletion of the helpers and tracker pair. Host drawing then runs only when the line renderer reports itself visible. Explicit UpdateLines can refresh the drawing without the host and visibility gates.

Deleting either endpoint removes the stored joint and both trackers’ attachment helper objects; the normal created pair leaves the original connected objects in the scene. Prepare dedicated helpers and reciprocal counterpart references. Assigning these fields does not itself create a physical connection, and the visual attachment positions are not a live replacement for its physical anchors.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.ControllerRig
member.summary: Stores controller input and body-tracking state for the player rig, with separate control roles for movement and for turning, height adjustment, and jumping.

remarks.para: A rig is a set of transforms representing body joints. This base class holds the two controller references and input caches; OpenControllerRig supplies the normal VR polling and tracked-pose updates. The base class itself does not read thumbsticks or fit a new avatar in SetAvatar.

Primary and secondary are control roles, not fixed left and right hands. In OpenControllerRig, ordinary right-handed thumbstick controls use the left controller for primary movement and the right controller for secondary turning, height adjustment, and jumping; the handedness setting swaps them. Touchpad devices have additional mappings.
