Runtime cleanup instead notifies break listeners and removes the component; explicit runtime Destroy uses its distinct destroy listeners. These callbacks are registered code called with the MarrowJoint to report or carry out work.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.MarrowLayers
member.summary: Unity layer indices for separating Marrow body, interaction and tracking shapes in collision filtering and physics queries.

remarks.para: A GameObject is one object in a Unity scene. A collider supplies its collision/detection shape. A physics query asks which shapes match a search. A layer mask is the set of categories that search is allowed to consider. Each bit is a yes/no switch selecting one category. The << operator selects the bit at the stated layer index, and | combines the selected bits so either category can match. For example, (1 << 18) | (1 << 19) = 262144 | 524288 = 786432; all these mask values are unitless. Here the football is the player’s sphere used for ground contact and movement.

A layer is a category assigned to a GameObject; colliders on that object belong to its category. These unitless values are indices, not distances or bit flags. A GameObject has one layer. Components supply the shape, movement, grabbing or tracking behavior, while layer collision settings and query masks decide which categories can be considered together.

A layer mask uses one bit per index: 1 << (int)MarrowLayers.Plug selects layer 19, and 1 << (int)MarrowLayers.Socket selects layer 18. Combine those masks with | to query both. Do not OR the enum indices themselves: 18 | 19 is 19, which gives just the Plug index. Default has index 0 but its mask is 1; a mask of 0 selects nothing.

MarrowBody.GatherColliders preserves its recognized special body layers, including Player, Interactable, Socket, Plug and the football categories. It assigns ordinary gathered colliders Default in its static/kinematic body branch, or Dynamic when the body's cached Rigidbody is non-kinematic. A Rigidbody is the physics-body component attached to an object; kinematic means its movement is controlled directly.

Tracker settings generate separate Entity, Being and Observer trigger shapes on layers 26, 27 and 28. Their corresponding volume categories are EntityTrigger 29, BeingTrigger 30 and ObserverTrigger 3. Zone handling still requires the Tracker to be found in its lookup with its cached hasBody and hasEntity flags true. A Tracker links an overlap-detection shape to a MarrowBody, the physical part, and its MarrowEntity, the object grouping those parts. Registered means that the Tracker is available in the game’s Tracker lookup. Tracker.Awake, Unity’s initialization callback (a routine called to perform or report an action), registers the Tracker and sets its cached hasBody and hasEntity flags from the body and entity references present then. Zone requires those two flags to be true; its overlap handler does not check the current validity of those references again. Tracker.Validate assigns the references without refreshing these flags. Choosing a number does not create the needed components or configure a collision pair.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.OverlapStateHelper
member.summary: Lets the overlap manager end an object's recorded trigger overlaps when that object is disabled.

remarks.para: A GameObject is Unity's container for a scene object and its components. A collider is the shape used to detect contact; a trigger is a collider that reports overlap without blocking movement. An overlap means that a trigger volume and another object intersect. The manager counts the recorded contacts so that several colliders between the same two GameObjects still form one logical overlap. This helper is a small component on the other object; the manager keeps the counts and relationships rather than storing them inside the helper.

When a new recorded pair begins, the manager adds OverlapStateHelper to the other GameObject if that object has neither an OverlapTrigger component nor this helper already. An object with OverlapTrigger uses its own matching disable path. You do not need to add a new helper for every collider contact.

OnDisable, Unity's disable callback, asks the manager to clear this GameObject's recorded relationships. A callback is a routine called to perform or report an action. For example, making a crate inactive while it is inside a recorded trigger overlap lets the manager end that relationship without requiring the crate to move out first.

Cleanup reduces affected recorded pair counts, then the manager dispatches queued OnOverlapExit notifications with the other GameObject argument when it processes the event queue. It does not directly call the trigger's exit logic from this helper or promise an exact frame delay. Already queued notifications are retained.

Adding or enabling this component alone does not scan nearby colliders or create overlap records. The inspected helper has only its disable notification; ordinary trigger-enter reporting creates the manager's records. Disabling only the helper can clear those records while the physical colliders remain where they are.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.OverlapTrigger
member.summary: Turns Unity collider enter and exit reports into counted, overridable GameObject overlap callbacks.

remarks.para: A GameObject is a scene object that holds components. A Collider is the component that defines a shape for physics contacts. A trigger volume detects objects overlapping its shape. This component forwards OnTriggerEnter and OnTriggerExit reports to OverlapTriggerManager using the other collider's own GameObject. The manager records a count for each trigger-GameObject and other-GameObject pair. The first recorded enter starts a logical overlap, and the last recorded exit ends it.

A Rigidbody is Unity's component for an object's movement in the physics simulation. A MarrowEntity is the game's entity component for an object and its parts. Several collider reports involving the same two GameObjects are combined by that count. Different child GameObjects are separate partners even when they share a parent Rigidbody or MarrowEntity, because this code uses collider.gameObject rather than either owning root. For example, two colliders on one crate GameObject share one counted relationship; colliders on two different crate children can produce separate relationships.

OnOverlapEnter and OnOverlapExit are virtual callbacks, routines called to perform or report an action. The manager queues them for all OverlapTrigger components on the trigger GameObject and calls them when it drains that queue. Their argument is the other GameObject. Count changes occur before queued callback dispatch, and there is no promised one-frame delay.

The base versions log messages naming the trigger and other object. A derived component is a component based on this class; overriding means replacing these callback methods with its own reactions. A derived component can override them to implement its intended gameplay reaction. For example, an implementation could record which partner GameObjects are present when enters arrive and remove those partners when exits arrive; it should not assume every collider report produces a separate callback.

OnDisable asks the manager to end recorded relationships for this GameObject, including when objects are disabled while still touching a volume. Cleanup can queue exit notifications that the manager later delivers even to a disabled component; it does not cancel previously queued notifications. On the other object, the manager normally adds OverlapStateHelper if it has neither that helper nor an OverlapTrigger, so disabling that partner can also end the recorded relationship.

The component relies on valid collider reports and an available overlap-manager plugin. Adding or enabling it alone does not scan for nearby overlaps or recreate records that disable cleanup already cleared. The counted records and queued callbacks describe reported overlap state; they do not themselves apply forces or choose a gameplay action beyond the base logging behavior.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.OverlapTriggerManager
member.summary: Turns collider contact reports into object-level overlap notifications and cleans up pairs when objects are disabled.

remarks.para: A collider is a shape Unity uses to detect contacts between objects. A trigger detects an overlap rather than pushing objects apart. OverlapTrigger reports the other collider’s GameObject to this manager. The manager counts contacts per trigger GameObject and other GameObject so several colliders can produce one logical enter and, after the final contact ends, one logical exit for each trigger component.

The manager changes its pair records immediately and queues the notifications. Its routine registered with Marrow’s normal update stage later calls the trigger’s OnOverlapEnter or OnOverlapExit with the other object. These callbacks are routines invoked to report the change; the base trigger routines log it, while overriding implementations can respond with their own behavior.

A reverse association and, when needed, an OverlapStateHelper allow DisableOverlap to clear existing pairs when either object is disabled. This can queue an exit without requiring physical movement out of the trigger. Pair cleanup does not cancel notifications already in the queue.

Access the registered manager through Instance after the plugin system is available. Its lookup does not create a new manager or scan the scene for nearby objects; ordinary contact reports create the records.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.PolyLineData
member.summary: Stores precomputed local path samples and spacing metadata for a PolyLine component.

remarks.para: This is a ScriptableObject, a Unity asset object that holds data separately from a scene component. A polyline is a path described by ordered sampled points. polyVerts provides those points and their directions, segmentResolution chooses the nominal distance step, and totalDistance carries supplied total-distance metadata.

Assign a prepared asset to PolyLine.lineData before the component's Awake, Unity's initialization callback. A callback is a routine called to perform or report an action. With a nonempty vertex table, PolyLine keeps its array reference and copies the spacing and total-distance scalars. This startup path consumes existing samples; it does not create or bake a new table.

Vertex positions are local to the consuming PolyLine Transform, using Unity distance units. The spacing choices return 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, or 1 unit; their millimeter-to-meter names assume one unit represents one meter. Keep the array geometry and nominal spacing consistent. The stored total-distance value is separate metadata, not a length recalculated by this asset's method.

SplineJoint uses PolyLine queries to place its generated physics contacts along a path, so the sampled geometry can guide a connected body. A physics contact here is a helper object with a physics body and a joint connection to the body being guided. A joint is a physics connection that limits how the two bodies move. For example, a prepared table can describe the local shape of a rail; the consuming PolyLine Transform places that shape in the scene, and a SplineJoint uses queried points for its contact targets.

Editing a vertex inside the shared table can affect subsequent queries, while replacing the entire asset array does not redirect already initialized components to it. Resolution and total-distance edits also leave initialized scalar copies unchanged. An empty table does not supply a replacement path in the inspected nearest-point and linear-distance routines. Prepare valid entries and metadata before relying on the path queries.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.PolyLineVert
member.summary: One stored sample of a PolyLine path, containing its location and the directions needed to find and orient points along that path.

remarks.para: position is relative to the PolyLine object's origin and axes, in Unity distance units before the object's Transform scale is applied. tangent gives the direction along the path; normal supplies an up reference for orientation. These directions are also stored in the line object's axes. PolyLine.GetPointAtIndex converts the stored position and directions to world coordinates, and SplineJoint uses the resulting path orientation to align its physics connection.

forward and backward are separate search directions. The nearby-point search uses them to choose a neighboring sample and project a point onto the path between samples. IsPointInDirection tests whether the displacement from position to the supplied point points toward the selected forward or backward direction. Supply that point in the same local coordinates as position: a point exactly at position, or exactly sideways to the selected direction, does not pass this test.

Changing position changes the sample's path location; changing tangent or normal changes the orientation data returned there; changing forward or backward changes the direction tests and projections. IsPointInDirection reads these stored values directly, so moving position does not automatically recalculate any of the direction vectors.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.RigidbodySettings
member.summary: Configures a physics body’s balance point, rotational resistance, spin limit, enable-time reset and collision-ignore pairs.

remarks.para: A Rigidbody is the Unity physics component that gives an object mass and motion; a collider supplies its contact shape. Attach this component alongside a Rigidbody and configure its fields before initialization. Provide a nonnull collidersToIgnore array before Start, even when no pairs should be ignored; use an empty array for that case. A null array causes a null-reference failure during startup. Awake (Unity’s initialization callback, a routine called to perform initialization) captures the original pose/mass and applies inertia/spin settings, OnEnable (the routine Unity calls when this component becomes enabled) stops motion and optionally restores pose or scales mass, and Start (the routine Unity calls for this component’s first startup) applies the center-of-mass and collision settings.

These settings are applied at their specific lifecycle stages rather than continuously. The public helpers can reapply the center or collision pairs later. The float velocity helpers add random spin changes; their names do not mean they assign a final movement speed.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.SoftSplineJointLimit
member.summary: Stores the boundary distance and response settings for limited sideways movement in a spline joint.

remarks.para: A spline is a curved path. SplineJoint guides a physical body along that path using generated Contact connections; here a Contact is a physics helper, rather than a collider touching something. With one Contact, its configured linear Y/Z settings describe sideways movement in the connection’s own axis frame.

limit is the linear boundary distance in meters, bounciness is the unitless rebound amount, and contactDistance is the tolerance in meters just inside that boundary. These values are copied into Unity’s linearLimit on the created ConfigurableJoint, a connection that constrains physical bodies. They do not describe an angular bend or the spring/damping drive coefficients.

The sideways motion must be Limited for this boundary to permit and restrict travel. Locked motion prevents travel; the Two- and Four-contact setup paths use Locked sideways motion and zero values instead of this configured struct. The chosen values are setup inputs, and editing them afterward does not automatically change the existing connections.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.SplineJoint
member.summary: Guides a physics body along a curved path using one, two or four generated contact constraints.

remarks.para: A Rigidbody is a body simulated by Unity physics. Each Contact creates a separate controlled physics body and a joint connecting it to the main body; a joint constrains how the bodies move relative to each other. The solver updates those contact targets along the PolyLine path, while linear drives push or resist travel and angular drives correct twisting or sideways tilt.

One uses the configured anchor and motion restrictions directly. Two spreads contacts front/back using _size.y, the configured front/back distance in metres. Four also spreads them sideways using _size.x, the configured side-to-side distance in metres. These are generated constraint layouts, not counts of collision points.

Awake is Unity’s initialization callback: a routine Unity calls to prepare the component when it is first initialized. Configure the body, path, count, anchors and restrictions before it creates contacts. Changing saved drive coefficients later requires RefreshContactConfig; the public drive setters instead update the live contacts without changing those saved fields. Count, anchor geometry, motion modes and limits are copied at setup and are not rebuilt by enabling the component or refreshing drives.

Update solves while the main body is not sleeping, meaning physics has temporarily stopped updating a resting body. PlaceOnSpline directly assigns a body Transform pose—the object’s position and orientation, because Transform stores position, rotation and scale—using the live spline curve; normal solving uses the baked PolyLine samples, the precomputed stored path points and directions. The Two/Four solver can also directly correct a body whose travel direction has reversed.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.SplineJointMotion
member.summary: Chooses whether a generated spline contact blocks sideways translation or allows it within a distance boundary.

remarks.para: A joint is a physics connection that constrains how objects move relative to one another. In Contact construction, this enum selects the joint's Y and Z translation modes: Locked blocks those sideways translations, while Limited permits them within the joint's shared linear-distance limit. X is the path-travel direction and uses separate settings. Rotation also has its own settings.

SplineJoint uses the configured _linearYZMotion only when creating its ContactCount.One layout. The Two and Four layouts create contacts with Locked sideways motion directly. This is one exclusive choice, not flags to combine, and the enum has no Free option. The inspected Contact constructor treats an unrecognized raw value through its Locked branch.

Configure the choice before Awake, Unity's initialization callback; a callback is a routine called to perform or report an action. Existing contacts keep the motion policies installed at construction. Joint drives apply forces that push or turn the body toward target motion. RefreshContactConfig updates drive speeds and strengths rather than these policies, so a later enum edit alone does not switch a live joint between locked and limited translation.

For example, a single-contact rail guide can block sideways sliding with Locked or permit bounded sideways offset with Limited, while separate X settings govern travel. The limited boundary is a shared distance from the joint origin, measured in Unity scene distance units; single-contact endpoint handling can replace that distance when limiting X, which also changes the active Y/Z boundary. Neither enum value means the object must hold one fixed position on the entire curve.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.Tracker
member.summary: Connects a , an invisible overlap-detection shape, to its owning , one physics unit, and , the group of an object’s bodies and interaction state, so zones can track their presence.

remarks.para: A collider is an invisible physics shape; a trigger collider reports overlaps without blocking movement. Tracker setup selects a trigger shape, records its MarrowBody and MarrowEntity owners, and places its GameObject in a shared lookup during Awake, Unity’s initialization routine. A body is one physics unit; an entity groups the object’s bodies and interaction state.

When that shape overlaps a zone, the zone looks up the tracker and counts its body and entity as present. Multiple trackers for one owner contribute to a shared count, so the owner is considered to leave when its final tracker exits. Both ownership snapshots, hasBody and hasEntity, must be true for that zone path.

Trackers also hold disable callbacks, routines registered to report deactivation with their collider argument. Body processing calls them when switching a tracker object off, allowing a zone to process departure. Tracker.OnDestroy instead removes its cache entry and clears the routines; it does not dispatch them itself.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.TrackerSettings
member.summary: Stores one shape, category and inclusion choice used to prepare a MarrowBody’s invisible overlap-detection tracker.

remarks.para: A Tracker is a component on a child object, with a collider that describes the space to test for overlaps. A collider is a shape used by Unity’s physics system; the prepared tracker colliders are marked as triggers so other objects can pass through them. This settings object is input to generation and preparation, rather than the live collider itself. A TrackerSettingsGroup supplies an array of these entries to a MarrowBody.

MarrowBody preparation gathers its ordinary colliders, calculates body bounds, then generates trackers. The body bounds are the enclosing box calculated from the body’s gathered ordinary collision shapes. They provide a center offset relative to the body and full X, Y and Z lengths, rather than an absolute position in the scene. Generation considers entries with isActive true; Bounds entries also need gathered ordinary colliders. Category layer values Entity = 1, Being = 2 and Observer = 4 select Unity layers EntityTracker = 26, BeingTracker = 27 and ObserverTracker = 28. Matching direct child Trackers can be reused, new children are attached at local zero position and identity rotation (no rotation relative to the parent), and unused candidate children are removed. Existing Plug-layer trackers are retained separately.

Bounds and Box prepare box colliders from MarrowBody.Bounds; the inspected Box branch does not read the stored size or center fields. Sphere uses center and radius. Capsule uses center, radius, height and direction, where direction chooses its local long axis and height includes its rounded ends. Distances use Unity distance units, interpreted as metres by Unity’s physics convention. Sphere and Capsule preparation divide center by the effective scale along each axis, and multiply radius, and capsule height, by the largest reciprocal scale component. Unequal scales therefore need not yield the nominal configured size in the scene.

For example, before preparation an included Entity-category Sphere entry with radius 0.5 describes a nominal half-unit detection radius. At tracker scale (2, 2, 2), preparation proposes collider-local radius 0.25 to compensate for scaling. This is an illustrative configuration, rather than a requirement for every tracker. The native new-settings constructor starts with isActive true, category 1, Bounds type, radius 0.5, height 2 and XAxis direction; serialized entries can replace these values.

Editing these fields only edits stored settings. It does not automatically regenerate child objects, update an existing collider, or set a tracker GameObject’s active state. When Sphere or Capsule center is reapplied, the preparation code compares old and proposed vector lengths: it can leave an old offset in place when only its direction changes. The individual fields describe the shape-specific formulas and update conditions.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Interaction.TrackerSettingsGroup
member.summary: Groups entries used to build a body's detection trackers, with category metadata.

remarks.para: A Tracker is a gameplay component with a collider, a physics shape used to detect contacts, and references to its owning body and entity. This settings group is data for MarrowBody.trackerSettings that Unity can save and load. Its settings array contains candidate detection volumes, while layers stores a group-level category declaration.

The inspected MarrowBody.GenerateTrackers method reads individual active entries and their layer values. Those values choose the Entity, Being, or Observer tracker collision layer; the group's layers mask is not a generation filter in that path. A category mask stores category choices that can be combined in one value. For example, adding an active Observer entry can produce an Observer tracker during generation without changing the group mask first.

Direct children are objects immediately one level beneath the body. Generation reuses or creates direct child tracker objects, validates their trigger colliders, preserves Plug-layer trackers, removes unused candidates, and records the resulting array on the body. Bounds is the recorded enclosing box of the body's gathered physics shapes. Bounds entries need ordinary body colliders; explicit shape entries can be processed without them. The checked Box branch also uses recorded body bounds, with object-scale adjustment, rather than the entry's size, although it has that explicit-shape eligibility. Sphere and Capsule use their configured measurements. A trigger detects overlap rather than provides a solid surface.

The constructor creates one active Bounds entry marked Entity and sets layers to Entity. Editing that mask later does not repopulate settings. Likewise, changing settings data alone does not apply new geometry to live trackers; the body's validation or generation path must process it. Keep the group and its entries valid before that operation.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.InteractionOptions
member.summary: Combinable options controlling selection, transfer and controller-specific release behavior for a .

remarks.para: These are independent bits stored in Grip.gripOptions: MultipleHands = 1, ToggledGrip = 2, FarHover = 4 and SwitchHands = 8. Combine the choices with bitwise OR. For example, MultipleHands | FarHover includes both choices (numeric value 5); assigning FarHover by itself replaces the set with just that choice. A zero value includes none of these four optional behaviors.

MultipleHands lets the nearby-hover search consider the same grip already held by the other hand. Far-hover means pointing toward a distant grip. FarHover allows the distant-hover search to consider the grip, with separate hand, receiver, host, aim and obstruction conditions; actual pulling needs additional action handling. The receiver is the component accepting hand interactions; its host is the object the grip belongs to. SwitchHands makes the target grip release its existing hands before a requested new attachment. When MultipleHands and SwitchHands are combined, the first affects selection while the second still controls attachment transfer.

ToggledGrip’s special held-release path applies to ViveWands controllers. It uses the secondary interaction button’s release report and a remembered initial-input flag so the first release can leave the grip attached; a later release after that flag clears detaches it. Other controller types retain their ordinary release test. These options are conditions read by interaction routines: editing the flags does not itself grab, pull, transfer or immediately detach a hand.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.InterpRig
member.summary: Blends tracked body poses and animated skeleton transforms for the rig pipeline’s physics updates.

remarks.para: The tracked body samples and the animated skeleton are stored separately. OnEarlyUpdate keeps the previous/new remapped BodyPose contents. A BodyPose groups body rotations, limb-extension values and other pose data; remapped means adapted to the avatar’s proportions. OnUpdate saves the supported animated transforms into lastRig after physics time advances. OnFixedUpdate blends those endpoints into this rig’s bodyPose and body transforms.

For a positive controller-sample interval, the fraction is (physicsTime − previousSampleTime) / (currentSampleTime − previousSampleTime). All three times are in seconds: physicsTime is Time.fixedTimeAsDouble, and the sample times are the controller rig’s previous/current pose timestamps. The resulting fraction is unitless. At 0 it selects the older endpoint, at 1 the newer, and at 0.5 halfway. The fraction is not clamped, so values beyond the endpoints extrapolate: they continue the blend past one of the two samples rather than stay between them. A zero or negative sample interval instead selects fraction 1.

For example, sample times 1.00 and 1.02 seconds with physics time 1.01 give 0.5. Those are illustrative times, not a promised timestep. The saved rig, manager, buffers and required skeleton references must be configured. RigManager dispatches these callbacks, meaning routines called to perform initialization or update actions; they are not independent Unity update loops. Its Awake, Unity’s initialization callback, invokes OnAwake to initialize the time marker.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Inventory
member.summary: Manages named inventory-slot notifications and separate body and utility holster placement groups.

remarks.para: An InventorySlot holds a reference to an item in a holster and reports insertion or removal. A SlotContainer describes where a holster sits on the player body. bodySlots and specialItems contain these placement containers; m_InventorySlots provides names for finding the slots that report item changes. Registering a name and configuring a container are separate operations.

Register a valid InventorySlot under a name, then use SubscribeToInsert or SubscribeToRemove to attach a callback, a routine called to perform or report an action. Each callback receives the slot. Insertion listeners see its newly stored item reference; removal listeners see the old reference before it is cleared or replaced. Match subscriptions with unsubscriptions when your listener is no longer needed.

FlipSlot has independent body and special-item choices. For ready, flippable body containers, it restores or negates the angle saved during initialization and writes the result to the current placement setting. It selects the left or right forearm region for ready special containers. It does not itself write object positions; PhysicsRig.SetBodySlot uses those settings for avatar placement. Prepare valid containers before changing handedness settings, and keep the dictionary and arrays consistent with the objects you intend to use.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.InventorySlot
member.summary: A component that records an item GameObject and reports changes to that record.

remarks.para: For example, Hand attachment code records the held object’s host GameObject in its slot. The slot itself is a small record and notification point; physical attachment and item movement are handled by the surrounding systems.

Insertion stores the new item before its insertion callbacks run. Removal callbacks run while the old item is still recorded, before clearing or replacement. Each callback receives the slot so it can inspect itemGameObject; a callback is a routine called to perform or report an action.
Direct Insert into an occupied slot requires an assigned removal callback. Remove can clear a slot without any listener. Writing itemGameObject directly skips the notifications.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.LadderInfo.Source
member.summary: Labels the source category stored with a ladder report: left hand 0, right hand 1, or feet 2.

remarks.para: LadderInfo combines this category with a rung reference and ladder dimensions. GetLadderInfo and the LadderInfo constructor copy the supplied category; PhysicsRig.UpdateLadderInfo stores the complete report before setting onLadder to 1. These are separate values, not flags to combine with bitwise operations.

The checked foot-collision reporter supplies FEET. The ladder controller’s physics-update reporter supplies LEFTHAND’s value 0 for its selected attached hand without choosing between left and right. Its label therefore does not guarantee detected hand identity. A physics update is a step of the movement and collision simulation.

Changing only the category does not create contact or attach a limb. The checked LadderForce movement-assistance routine reads the saved rung information without branching on source; this statement applies to that complete routine, not every possible reader of LadderInfo.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.LateReferences.LateReferenceManager
member.summary: Finds objects by the ID stored in a and delivers indexed objects to references waiting for a linking pass.

remarks.para: A late reference saves an ID instead of requiring its target object to be available immediately. An export table pairs those IDs with existing Unity objects. This shared manager keeps dictionaries—collections that look up a value by a key—for ID-to-object, object-to-ID, owning-table, and waiting-reference information.

LoadTable indexes a scene table's current exports. TryGetObject reads an indexed ID and checks the requested object type. Register writes a reference's current object into a table and the object caches. AddSubscription queues a reference; LinkSubscribedLateReferences runs a separate pass to deliver available cached objects and remove processed waiting groups.

For example, a reference expecting a Light can wait under door-switch-01. Index a scene table containing that ID and a Light, then run the linking pass. A compatible reference stores that Light, marks itself linked, and calls its linking event. Merely loading a table or adding the subscription does not perform that pass.

SceneExportTable indexes itself during Awake, Unity's initialization call, and removes its current entries when destroyed. LinkLateReferenceSubscriptions runs cleanup and then linking during its own Awake. For explicit setup, arrange indexing before the linking pass; these routines do not provide a continuous per-frame retry service.

The caches must agree about each ID and its owner, and exported IDs should be unique across loaded tables. UnloadTable removes lookup entries without clearing objects already stored in linked references. VacuumLinks removes stale IDs but can fail during reverse-key cleanup; waiting references and current table exports are separate state.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Magazine
member.summary: Controls a physical magazine’s stored ammunition, decorative cartridge models, grab handling and plug insertion.

remarks.para: A component is behavior attached to a Unity scene object. This one has a magazine state data object holding capacity settings and one cartridge entry per usable round, a hand grip, an interaction host for its physical parts, and an ammo plug for connecting to a gun or ammo receiver.

Initialization sets the ammunition and asynchronously loads up to two decorative rounds at the magazine opening. Asynchronous loading can pause until an asset is ready while the game continues. The display models do not add usable ammunition. Count refreshes show neither model for zero rounds, only the first for one round, and both for two or more, when their setup and visibility gates allow it.

The first initialization marks setup started before visual loading finishes. Await the original InitializeAsync task to know when its work finishes; the started flag and another initialization call cannot confirm that completion.

An unclaimed grab can register this magazine with the player’s ammo receiver and credit its configured capacity, in whole rounds, to the available ammo inventory. Claim() only marks the claim flag. The plug’s completion callbacks update the insertion flag before requesting cartridge hiding or showing.

Pool setup, which prepares a reusable object, connects listeners, refills ammunition and resets tracking flags. Cleanup disconnects listeners and receiver tracking, clears cached art references, cleans up the plug and permits a new initialization. Provide the state, capacity settings, plug and interaction host before those paths run.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.MagazineState
member.summary: Stores a magazine’s loaded ammunition list, default ammunition type and capacity configuration for detachable magazines or an internal gun feed.

remarks.para: This is a data container, not a scene object that moves or fires bullets. Each list entry represents one loaded round by referring to its shared CartridgeData ammunition definition. AmmoCount is the whole-number list length; magazineData.rounds is the configured whole-number capacity. A gun stores its chambered round separately.

Construction creates an empty list. Assign magazineData before filling, then use Initialize to store a default ammunition type and load a starting count. Refill later replaces the entire load with the current default. Changing configuration alone leaves existing entries unchanged.

The list takes rounds from the end. AddCartridge can append a different ammunition type without replacing earlier entries; PullCartridge takes the newest remaining entry. For example, three type-A entries followed by two type-B entries are pulled as B, B, A, A, A.

The optional onAmmoChange callback is a function registered for count notifications, and it runs immediately when an operation calls it. Initialize, Refill and AddCartridge notify after their work. SetCartridge skips the notification when its requested count already equals the current count. A successful PullCartridge and ClearMagazine do not notify; an empty pull notifies with zero. Physical cartridge visuals are managed by the separate Magazine component.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.MarrowSDK
member.summary: Provides shared SDK version checks, mod storage paths, and text-cleanup helpers for the Marrow runtime.

remarks.para: SDK means software development kit, the tools and shared code for making content. This runtime class stores this build’s SDK version 1.2.0 and initial minimum version 0.6.0. Its compatibility check accepts major/minor versions between those bounds, including the ends and ignoring patch numbers.

It caches paths under the game’s persistent saved-data folder for Mods, ModsStaging, com.unity.addressables asset-cache data, and settings_mods.json. Startup computes the strings; reading the mods and staging path properties also creates their directories if missing.

The text helpers have different purposes. SanitizeID keeps ASCII letters, digits, and periods for content identifiers. SanitizeName removes the platform’s filename-invalid characters plus square brackets and hyphens from names. For example, My Mod_2! becomes MyMod2 as an identifier, while Puzzle-[Pack] becomes PuzzlePack as a name.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.OpenController
member.summary: Adapts this hand’s game input into saved buttons, finger bends, grip tests, gestures, and vibration requests.

remarks.para: Set up left/right handedness, the controller rig, and game input sources before using the normal update path. OnUpdate copies input and then calculates finger curls, solved grip, and grab/release/menu-tap flags. A curl or squeeze is a unitless amount, usually 0 open to 1 fully bent or squeezed.

Button getters return saved input; they do not poll hardware or perform a gameplay action themselves. Down/up flags describe an input change copied into an update, while a held flag can stay true across updates. Grab flags describe squeeze input rather than proof that an object was successfully held.

GetGesturePose performs its own gesture classification when requested and normally keeps the result for 0.2 unscaled seconds, independent of slow motion. HapticAction forwards a vibration request to the selected hand’s input source.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.OpenControllerRig
member.summary: Player controller rig that turns VR device input and tracked poses into movement controls and a fitted tracking-avatar body.

remarks.para: A rig is the grouped player-body and controller setup. A pose is position plus orientation. A Transform stores position, orientation and scale. Calibration records tracker-to-body corrections in child objects directly beneath the raw trackers; each child’s local coordinates use its containing tracker’s origin and axes. OpenControllerRig extends ControllerRig. RigManager calls its initialization and update slots, meaning the virtual routines assigned to those stages. During Awake, Unity’s initialization callback or routine, it links the controller components to the rig, prepares its RealHeptaAvatar measurements and registers a readiness routine. Once MarrowGame is ready, it registers a camera-render callback: a routine called for a rendering action.

Its early update maps physical left and right controllers into movement/time-control and turn/height roles, handles platform pause, blends tracking changes and fits the body. An active RigManager.activeSeat receives both axis vectors first, each containing two unitless stick or pad values; when its handler accepts them, the rig zeroes both caches and clears movement-active state. Ordinary turning requires no active seat. OpenController touch state is true for device-reported joystick touch or unitless radial stick deflection greater than 0.5, meaning farther than halfway from center toward the usual full input range of 1; touch and button press are separate inputs.

It supports snap and smooth turning, selectable movement-direction references and configured touchpad direction curves. The speed setting and snap-angle mode are separate controls. Curve input and output are angles in degrees while axis magnitude stays unitless; the assigned curve keys determine the response. The RealHeptaAvatar supplies the proportions and skeleton for fitting the tracked body and is separate from the manager’s equipped game avatar.

Optional body markers guide torso and limb fitting, with different gates for torso tracking, calibrated shoulder/elbow hints and the paired foot/knee path. Raw tracker transforms and their calibrated child markers must be assigned consistently; the capture routine requires those child objects and does not discover physical devices. The main-camera render hook refreshes late poses and calls onLastCameraUpdate, and destruction removes this rig’s render subscription.

For example, a mod can select head-relative movement with SetDirectionMasterTransform or provide correctly configured tracking markers and capture their calibration. The class exposes virtual rig hooks for customized behavior, but assigning a field does not automatically register a replacement rig, start a device stream or repeat initialization. Preserve the manager’s dispatch and the setup expected by any overridden stage.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.OpenControllerRig.CurveMode
member.summary: Chooses which configured curve the rig uses to remap active controller-input direction.

remarks.para: The six values select the existing preset references curve_Linear, curve_Poles, curve_Genesis, curve_Dpad, curve_SmoothGenesis and curve_SmoothDpad. OnStart, the rig’s startup routine, selects from the saved curveMode; SetTouchPadCurve selects the active reference immediately without rewriting that stored mode. Changing the field after startup therefore does not itself select a new active curve.

TouchPadCurve treats each configured curve as an angular mapping: input and output angles are degrees measured from upward input, positive toward the right, while this angular-mapping stage retains the unitless deflection magnitude supplied to it. Here deflection magnitude means how far the control input is pushed away from its center; it has no distance or time unit. Earlier input processing can change that magnitude. It affects direction rather than directly setting walking speed. Curve keys are configured points pairing an input angle with an output angle. The assigned keys determine the shape, and the checked evaluator needs a non-null curve.

For example, use SetTouchPadCurve(Dpad) to select the currently assigned Dpad preset. This enum does not supply the preset keys or force all thumbsticks through the mapping; the checked early-update consumer applies it when the primary movement input is marked active for processing, including thumbstick as well as touchpad controller branches. Later player-settings propagation can select another active curve.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.OpenControllerRig.DirectionMode
member.summary: Chooses the orientation source that uses for walking direction.

remarks.para: Controller selects physical left when isRightHanded is true and physical right otherwise; Head selects m_head; Custom selects CustomDirection. The chosen transform is cached in directionMasterTransform. Its world orientation and the body-support reference rotate active movement input; its position is not a destination.

OnStart selects from the stored directionMode. SetDirectionMasterTransform selects immediately without rewriting that saved mode, so changing the stored enum later does not itself replace the cached transform. For example, selecting Head makes subsequent active movement use the rig head’s orientation.

Movement axes are unitless input, not metre distances or walking speed. Supply the required transform before selection and movement. The startup missing-Custom fallback changes the stored mode to Head after attempting Custom, without recaching Head in that branch. Player settings can select the reference again later.

A Transform stores an object’s position, rotation and scale. Here the selected world rotation is compared with centerOfPressure, the rig Transform used as the body’s orientation base, before turning the walking input.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.ParticleSpreadManager.Info
member.summary: A saved orientation-and-angle record for one particle system configured by .

remarks.para: This is a class, an object holding a bundle of values. The manager stores the supplied surface-normal and incoming-direction arrows, their calculated reflection, a unitless emission-angle control value and the configured component's name. It creates the record after setting that particle system's world rotation and shape angle; this is not the position or travel state of an individual particle.

A normal points perpendicular to a surface, a direction describes the incoming arrow, and the reflected arrow mirrors that direction across the normal. The usual impact caller supplies these using world axes, the level's axes. The spread number is the cube of how closely the normal lines up with the reversed incoming arrow; a limited copy then blends between half the configured minimum and maximum angles, measured in degrees.

AutoOrient clears the manager's old records and creates new ones while processing its configured ParticleSpread components. For example, one impact can produce separate records labeled Sparks and Dust. The inspected manager methods do not reread these records to drive the effects, so changing a stored field does not reconfigure a particle system through those methods.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.PhysTorso
member.summary: Coordinates the five simulated torso bodies, seven joint controllers, collision shapes and hand grips for the player's physical body.

remarks.para: A Rigidbody is a physically simulated body; a Servo controls a physics joint, the connection applying forces between bodies. This component stores those existing objects for the head, neck, chest, spine and pelvis. It does not create them in its constructor. Configure the references before PhysicsRig, the component that simulates the whole player body, runs setup.

PhysicsRig.OnAwake asks it to disable four head/neck-to-spine collision pairs and registers the body and grip references. PhysicsRig.SetAvatar runs collider, joint and neck-grip calibration, matching geometry and saved drive settings to the avatar, the player's in-game body. Its SetBodyMassDistribution stage calculates a torso-mass share and passes it to SetTorsoMass, which apportions that amount across the five bodies. Friction changes install a configured physics material, the asset holding contact friction/bounce choices.

The four adjacent spine joints follow requested relative rotations during normal target updates and refresh angular drives during early updates when the scale markers change. A rotation target requests a pose; it does not immediately set the body's actual pose. The shutdown flag skips those normal methods while separate drive, target-reset, calibration and friction helpers remain callable.

Rigidbody mass is commonly expressed in kilograms; linear velocity is in world-space Unity distance units per second, and the Unity-unit-to-metre conversion depends on scene scale. Joint and collider dimensions use their configured local or world distance frames. Strength and damping multipliers are unitless. Saved calibration values, later scale fields and current physical state are separate, so changing a setting does not automatically rebuild the configured body.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.PlayerDamageReceiver
member.summary: Receives attacks on a player body part and forwards them, together with that part's label, to its assigned component.

remarks.para: This Unity component connects a body part's hit detection to the player's health handler. Give each receiver the appropriate bodyPart label, such as Head or Chest. During the health component's Awake startup hook, receivers found under the player's PhysicsRig are connected to that health component. PhysicsRig is the player-body setup used for physical movement and collisions.

Received attacks have their hit origin and surface normal changed from scene coordinates to coordinates relative to the receiver before health is called. The receiver leaves the separate attack direction and the damage amount unchanged. The health handler can then apply its body-part rules, optional hit marks, and health-state rules.

Unity's collision-entry notification reports when a physical contact begins. This receiver forwards that notification with its part label only while the receiver is enabled. Its attack method has no matching enabled check: code that calls ReceiveAttack directly can still send an attack through a disabled receiver. Attacks and collision reports therefore have separate forwarding conditions.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.PlayerDamageReceiver.BodyPart
member.summary: Chooses which player body region a damage receiver reports to its health handler.

remarks.para: Assign one value to PlayerDamageReceiver.bodyPart for the region that receiver covers. A receiver is the component that forwards a hit to its assigned Health component. ReceiveAttack reads the current label on each call; changing the label alone does not cause a hit, move a bone or reshape the collider, the physics detection shape. These are unitless identifiers, not distances, angles or values to combine as flags.

In the inspected Health.OnReceivedDamage path, Head sends incoming damage × 4.1 to TAKEDAMAGE and every other listed region sends incoming damage × 0.6. Incoming damage uses game health points; both multipliers are unitless. For example, the same incoming 10-point hit requests 41 points for Head or 6 points for Neck, torso or any limb. The handler requires alive to be true and ignores attacks whose backFacing marker is true. It does not assign separate health pools or limb-stun rules to these labels.

The visual-damage option separately uses the selected region’s stored position and orientation in the avatar’s reference pose only when Attack.OrderInPool is zero or negative; a positive value returns before the BodyPart switch. The receiver supplies hit coordinates relative to itself, and the selected stored transform maps them into the visual hit data. This visual path runs before the alive check, so the label does not by itself promise that a hit reduced health or produced a visible mark. Match labels to the physical receivers and prepare the Health and renderer references.

OnCollisionEnter, Unity’s routine called when a physics collision begins, also forwards the label when this receiver component is enabled. The inspected base Health.OnCollision routine is empty, so receiving a collision with a body-part label does not itself guarantee collision damage. A different health implementation can provide its own handling rules.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Player_Health
member.summary: Manages the player’s health, recovery, view feedback, dying state and final death. The static , and delegates are callback lists: routines that other code registers to receive reports of these changes.

remarks.para: Attack messages arrive through Health and reduce health through TAKEDAMAGE. In ordinary mortal mode, nonfatal damage restarts a delayed recovery and a view-border fade. The wait and recovery use game-time seconds, which run more slowly during slow motion. The visual effect is created from Vignetter and follows the main camera; several retained impact, prop and UI fields are not read by this implementation.

When mortal-mode health reaches zero, Dying marks deathIsImminent true before notifying OnDeathImminent(true) and starts a closing-eye countdown. LifeSavingDamgeDealt can cancel that state: it clears the flag before OnDeathImminent(false), then restores half of max_Health, the full-health amount in health points, after that notification and starts recovery. The registered character-death callback, a routine called to report a character’s death, also calls the save routine while death is imminent and the mode is not instant death. In instant-death mode, damage does not start ordinary regeneration, and the closing-eye countdown uses instaDeathTimeAmount in game-time seconds.

A callback is a routine called to report or perform an action. The damage callback receives the requested TAKEDAMAGE amount in health points after the base health operation and feedback scheduling. Final Death calls base Health first, making alive false and clearing deathIsImminent, then notifies OnPlayerDeath before starting the reload or checkpoint sequence. Changing reloadLevelOnDeath chooses between those two final paths.

The reload sequence waits one game-time second before requesting scene reload. The checkpoint sequence immediately queues a request to move the player’s body to the checkpoint. The body-control system applies that request during its next processing step. The sequence later calls Respawn after roughly one unscaled second; unscaled seconds advance at real-time speed. It holds that completion while the physical entity remains hibernating, meaning its physics is temporarily suspended. A coroutine is a sequence of work that continues across frames; a frame is one game update step.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Plugins.IMarrowPlugin
member.summary: Provides the load-stage contract that lets registered Marrow plugins finish initialization through before the framework marks them loaded.

remarks.para: A plugin is an extra piece of code that adds a feature. An interface is a contract that gives the framework a common way to call different plugin classes. This interface supplies a load callback, a method called at the plugin-initialization stage.

The callback returns a UniTask, a handle that tells the framework when its work has finished. The default method returns an already-completed task and does no plugin-specific setup. An implementation can replace that behavior with work that finishes immediately or continues later; there is no fixed waiting time.

The plugin manager creates and registers plugin instances, then dispatches the load stage. For each eligible registered plugin it waits for the callback’s task before marking that plugin loaded. The inspected dispatcher skips plugins marked running and does not use the loaded flag as a once-only guard. Implementing the interface alone does not register a new plugin instance.

For example, a registered plugin can prepare data needed by its feature in the load callback and return the task for that preparation. This contract describes initialization of the plugin, rather than confirmation that a game level finished loading. Plugin start, stop and level-change notifications have separate interfaces and callbacks.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Plugins.IMarrowPluginLevelCallbacks
member.summary: Defines callbacks that a plugin can use before and after a level loads or unloads; callback work may finish immediately or later.

remarks.para: A plugin is code that adds a feature to Marrow. An interface is a contract that lets the plugin manager call different plugin classes through the same methods, and a callback is a routine the plugin manager calls at one step of a level change. This interface extends IMarrowPlugin and provides virtual defaults for its four level callbacks. A plugin can override the stages it needs. The load callbacks take a LevelCrateReference, which identifies the level being loaded; the before-unload and after-unload callbacks take no arguments.

Each method returns a UniTask, a completion signal that tells the manager when that callback's work has finished. A callback may finish immediately or later. The default bodies return an already-completed task. When dispatching, MarrowPlugins calls the matching interface method and waits for its returned task before continuing to another plugin callback. No fixed delay or frame count is part of this contract.

In the inspected StreamSession.Load path, the framework loads the incoming scene, awaits the before-unload dispatch, unloads all other scenes and awaits those unload tasks, then awaits the after-unload dispatch. This is the observed order for that path, not a claim about every possible caller.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Pool.DespawnDelay
member.summary: Asks a pooled object to despawn after its configured scaled-time delay has elapsed.

remarks.para: The pool reuses objects instead of creating a fresh one for every use. A Poolee is the pool-tracking component attached to a reusable Unity object. During spawn setup, the pool assigns its ID before activating the object and calling pool initialization; deinitialization clears that ID. Each time it initializes this object for a spawn, this component records a new start time. Its per-frame Update waits until Poolee.ID is nonzero and the delay has elapsed, then calls Poolee.Despawn. A GameObject is Unity's scene object that holds components. That call runs the pool's despawn flow; for an active object, the inspected path deinitializes the object and turns it off.
The constructor sets the default delay to 1.0 scaled second. Slow motion lengthens the wait in real time, while a time-scale pause stops it.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Pool.Pool
member.summary: Manages Poolee instances created from a SpawnableCrate so they can be reused.

remarks.para: A Poolee is a component attached to a GameObject, the Unity object that holds components, to identify a pooled instance. A pool keeps three lists: _objects tracks managed instances, _spawned tracks instances checked out for use, and _despawned tracks returned instances available for reuse. These lists describe the pool’s state; they do not always match whether each GameObject is active in the scene.

Spawn returns a UniTask<Poolee>, an asynchronous task whose result is a Poolee. If the pool has a returned instance and forceInstantiation is false, it takes the first one from _despawned. Otherwise it loads a GameObject from the SpawnableCrate asset definition as needed and clones the cached inactive template. The selected object receives the requested world position and rotation, gets the optional local scale when one was supplied, is reparented to the requested Transform when needed, and is activated if inactive before its initialization callbacks run. If the template asset load returns null, that Spawn has no Poolee result.

A callback is a routine the game calls at a particular lifecycle moment. Despawn acts only on a Poolee found in _spawned: it invokes the despawn delegate with the GameObject, then calls the deinitialization method on each registered object implementing IPoolable (an interface objects implement to receive pool lifecycle calls). The delegate runs before deinitialization clears SpawnableCrate and before the _spawned/_despawned list transition, so listeners observe the pre-deinitialize, still-spawned state. Despawn then moves the instance to _despawned and disables its GameObject unless skipDisable is true. Clear removes an instance from all three lists but does not perform that lifecycle transition or destroy the object.

A prefab is the reusable GameObject template. The _parentTransform field stores the outer holder; during template loading, Spawn creates an inactive child container under it and places the cached template copy inside that container. The Spawn call’s separate parent argument controls the spawned or reused instance.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.Pool.SpawnEvents
member.summary: Abstract base component for responding to a Poolee’s initialize, spawn, and deinitialize stages and requesting despawns.

remarks.para: A pooled object is kept for reuse instead of being destroyed and recreated each time. SpawnEvents is a Unity component for a derived script attached to that scene object. Its serialized _poolee field points to the object’s Poolee. Reset can find that component on this GameObject or in its parent chain; Awake registers SpawnEvents in the Poolee’s IPoolable list. An interface is a list of methods a class agrees to provide; IPoolable lists the initialize, spawn, and deinitialize methods. A callback is a method Poolee calls at one of those stages so a registered component can respond.

The Poolee dispatches three distinct stages to registered components: initialize, spawn, and deinitialize. SpawnEvents’ base versions of those callbacks are empty, so a derived class must override the callback to perform its own work. ID reads the Poolee’s unsigned 64-bit identity value; IsDespawned reports whether that value is zero. Despawn forwards a request to the Poolee, which handles the pool-specific path.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.PrismaticSFX
member.summary: Plays Rigidbody movement sounds with speed-controlled volume, plus optional one-shot point triggers.

remarks.para: Place this component with its own Rigidbody, assign velocityTran as the measurement point, and provide nonnull modulatedClips and audioEvents arrays; empty arrays disable those choices. sourceTran selects the sound origin and defaults to this component’s Transform during Awake. An optional rb_parent subtracts motion at the same world point; an optional same-object InteractableHost supplies holding-hand vibration. Speeds are world units per second, or metres per second in a scene using one Unity unit per metre.

Each awake Update measures current point velocity, checks event triggers using the larger current/previous speed, saves the current sample, then processes modulated clips. Continuous volume uses current speed’s clamped minSpeed-to-maxSpeed fraction and approaches it by at most 25 × Time.deltaTime each frame. A sleeping body fades volume toward zero by at most 10 × Time.deltaTime, resets previous samples and rearms playback; a player reaching zero volume is stopped. Time.deltaTime is scaled elapsed seconds. OnDisable stops the managed sound, as does OnJointBreak unless _blockJointBreakStop is true. These stops do not reset the single-play latch or stop independent event sounds.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.PrismaticSFX.AudioEvent
member.summary: Stores one proximity-sound rule for PrismaticSFX: its trigger point and facing, clip choices, speed-to-volume range, distance threshold, and whether it may fire again.

remarks.para: PrismaticSFX.Update reads this serializable rule when checking for a sound. A Unity Transform gives an object a position and facing direction. eventTran sets the trigger center and facing direction; it is not the playback origin. The sound is requested at the PrismaticSFX component's sourceTran, with a zero local offset. An AudioClip is a stored sound recording; eventClip holds the choices, and Audio3dManager, the game's audio helper, picks a clip at random when the array is nonempty. A Rigidbody is Unity's physics body, and point velocity is that body's velocity at a chosen position; a rotating body can have different point velocities at different positions. velocityTran marks the point to measure. If rb_parent is assigned, the component subtracts that body's point velocity at the same point. It compares the larger magnitude from the current and previous frame velocity samples.

Before checking events, the component uses a Rigidbody path that skips sleeping bodies and requires effective speed to be strictly greater than the component-wide PrismaticSFX.minSpeed. Each AudioEvent then has its own minSpeed: speeds below that value skip the event, while equality passes this event-level test. This AudioEvent.maxSpeed is not a speed limit; it is the upper end of the event's clamped 0-to-1 volume multiplier, calculated from (effective speed - this event's minSpeed) / (this event's maxSpeed - this event's minSpeed). Equal event minSpeed and maxSpeed produce zero in this calculation. Speed uses Unity distance units per second, typically metres per second when one Unity unit represents one metre.

triggerDistance is a world-space distance in Unity scene units, typically metres when one Unity unit represents one metre. The update compares the squared distance from velocityTran.position to eventTran.position with triggerDistance squared: a true event must be strictly inside, and a false event is rearmed only when strictly outside. Equality at the boundary does neither. The event also skips motion that points partly along eventTran.forward (the direction the trigger faces); sideways or opposite motion passes this direction check. For the movement check, the update converts velocityTran.position into eventTran's local coordinates and skips when local Z is at least 2 × effective speed × Time.deltaTime. Local Z is the distance along eventTran's own Z axis from its origin; effective speed is in Unity distance units per second, Time.deltaTime is the current frame duration in seconds, and 2 is a dimensionless multiplier. With the usual one-unit-per-metre scene scale and an unscaled Transform, the right side is a distance in metres.

eventEnabled records whether this event may fire again; it is not a general sound on/off switch. The sequence is outside the trigger distance to arm, then pass the inside, speed, direction, and movement checks to request a sound. After requesting playback and completing any hand haptic calls (controller vibration), the same Update clears eventEnabled; it does not wait for the clip to finish. Audio3dManager starts playback separately and does not wait for it to finish. A false event already inside the trigger distance cannot fire until it first moves strictly outside and later re-enters.

The native AudioEvent constructor sets minSpeed to 1, maxSpeed to 4, and triggerDistance to 0.1. At the usual one-unit-per-metre scene scale these are 1 m/s, 4 m/s, and 0.1 m. That constructor does not assign eventEnabled, eventTran, or eventClip; serialized instance data or later setup may supply them, and this constructor alone does not establish values for any particular scene or prefab.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.ProjectileEmitter
member.summary: Static helper that registers projectiles with the shared spawn pool and emits them from a supplied Transform, Unity’s component that provides the projectile’s starting position and rotation.

remarks.para: The game type is static: nothing on it is placed in a scene, and both operations are plain method calls. The usual pattern is to call Register once during setup and then call Emit whenever the weapon fires. The game follows this itself — a turret registers its projectile from Awake only in its Cartridge fireType branch (value 0), and its fire handler calls Emit in that branch. Awake is Unity’s setup routine for this script component. Unity calls it once when an active object loads the component; if the object is inactive then, Unity calls it the first time the object becomes active. In the GachaLauncher branch (value 1), the turret instead registers and spawns separate Spawnable values directly through AssetSpawner. A Gun calls Emit from its own fire handler.

Neither call hands you a finished result. Register starts loading the crate’s prefab (the saved template Unity loads to create a crate object) asynchronously, without exposing its completion; the load may still be pending when it returns. Emit starts a pool spawn and neither returns the spawned object nor guarantees it exists before returning. When the spawned object does exist and carries a Projectile component, that component is initialized with the ProjectileData and with the TriggerRefProxy that was passed to Emit. Which and how many projectiles appear, and their spread, follow the data's emission settings (copy count, spread angle in degrees, start radius in Unity world units (normally meters under Unity’s default physics convention)) as interpreted by Emit.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.PuppetMasta.BaseEnemyConfig.HealthSettings
member.summary: Stores the health, collision-stun, recovery, and anger settings that BaseEnemyConfig copies into an enemy.

remarks.para: This object is configuration, not the enemy's current health or a running stun timer. BaseEnemyConfig.ApplyTo copies its values into the live SubBehaviourHealth object. Changing these stored values afterward requires applying the configuration again; copying health scales alone does not heal the enemy.

The live system keeps overall and limb health as fractions, recovers stun counters over game-time updates, and lets particular enemy behaviors change aggression during damage reactions. BaseEnemyConfig.ApplyFrom can copy the live settings, including the current aggression value, back into this object.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.PuppetMasta.BehaviourBase
member.summary: Provides ordered lifecycle and update hooks for behaviours controlling a simulated character body.

remarks.para: A behaviour is a Unity component that supplies the character’s reactions and control logic. A muscle here is one physics-controlled body part. A derived class replaces base hooks with its own logic; the base lifecycle hooks are empty until overridden.

Wrapper methods call optional pre-callbacks, the custom hook, then optional post-callbacks. A callback is a routine other code supplies to be called at that stage. Some wrappers require initialization and enabled, while the fixed, ordinary and late update wrappers can still call their hook when disabled once initialized with muscles. Initialized hit, collision, and collision-exit notifications also run their pre-callback, custom hook, and post-callback pattern; those wrappers require initialization but do not check enabled.

PuppetMaster discovers and initializes these behaviours, then calls the update/read/write wrappers at the appropriate stages of its own processing. A frame is one game update, and a physics step is one simulation step; they can occur at different rates. Pool registration and an animation contact-point logging tool are also provided.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.PuppetMasta.BehaviourBaseNav
member.summary: Abstract shared navigation and behavior-state base for concrete NPC behaviors.

remarks.para: This abstract class holds shared navigation state and a Unity NavMeshAgent. A NavMesh is Unity's navigation map of walkable scene surfaces; the agent calculates and follows a path to a destination. A Unity world position is in scene units, commonly treated as metres only when the scene uses a one-unit-per-metre scale.

The mental-state enum contains Rest, Roam, Investigate, Agroed, Engaged, and MindControlled. The class also has a separate locomotion-state layer. Derived behaviors provide the abstract SwitchMentalState and SwitchLocoState hooks; the enum names alone do not define every derived behavior's detailed response.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.PuppetMasta.BehaviourPuppet
member.summary: Component that manages balance and recovery for a physics-driven PuppetMaster character across , , and modes.

remarks.para: BehaviourPuppet is a Unity component in the PuppetMaster system. PuppetMaster connects an animated target to physics-driven muscle bodies. A Rigidbody is Unity’s component for a simulated physics body, including its mass and velocity. A joint connects one physics body to another, so muscle bodies act as linked body parts. Pinning is the physics force that helps a muscle follow its animated target.

In Puppet, the bodies follow the target with normal pinning. In Unpinned, the character becomes a ragdoll and normal pinning is released or reduced. In GetUp, the behavior aligns the target and blends toward a recovery animation. Use SetState to switch modes because it coordinates colliders, live muscle weights, timers, target alignment, and event order; the state property alone only stores the enum.

FixedUpdate work runs on Unity physics steps. Rigidbody velocity is measured in Unity world units per second, positions are in the Unity world-coordinate frame, and elapsed timers are in seconds. The reviewed game data does not prove that one Unity world unit equals one metre. Normalized weights and multipliers are unitless; no runtime unit or effect is established here for the separate top-level regainPinSpeed setting.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.PuppetMasta.Muscle
member.summary: One physical puppet limb driven by a configurable joint, a physics connection between bodies. Its joint drive uses the animated target's rotation to drive the physical body, while Map copies the physical pose (rotation, and position when Props.mapPosition is enabled) back onto the animated target when the effective mapping weight is positive.

remarks.para: One physical PuppetMaster limb record: it links an animated target Transform to a physical ragdoll bone, MarrowBody, and MarrowJoint, caches hierarchy/collider information, and supplies target poses and drive settings. Unity positions are metres, linear velocities are metres per second, elapsed times are seconds, and rotations are Quaternions unless an entry explicitly says degrees per second. Local space is relative to a Transform parent; world space is the scene frame; a joint frame is the ConfigurableJoint's own axes. The class coordinates these frames but does not create a Rigidbody or guarantee that a property assignment immediately changes physics.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.PuppetMasta.PuppetMaster
member.summary: Actively pinned ragdoll that follows an animated target. It kills, freezes and resurrects NPCs.
member.para: Ported from RootMotion's PuppetMaster. SLZ added pooling and animator culling for BONELAB NPCs.

remarks.para: A Unity component that coordinates an animated target with a physically simulated ragdoll. It owns Muscle joints, target-pose mapping, Animator parameter culling, pooling, solver references, teleport requests, and Alive/Dead/Frozen lifecycle transitions. Unity terms: a GameObject is a scene object that holds components, and a component supplies behavior attached to it; a Rigidbody is a physics body; a Transform stores position and orientation; and a ConfigurableJoint constrains two bodies. FixedUpdate uses Unity's fixed physics clock, Update runs on the rendered-frame clock, and LateUpdate/OnLateUpdate finish pose synchronization. Positions use metres, rotations use Quaternions, and pose snapshots use targetRoot-relative coordinates where described.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.PuppetMasta.SubBehaviourHealth
member.summary: Tracks overall and limb health, stun recovery, and how strongly an enemy's simulated body follows its intended pose.

remarks.para: The owning behavior drives this helper object. Health fractions are unitless, normally ranging from 0 for depleted to 1 for full. Stun counters are unitless recovery values that move toward 1 and can become negative: 1 means recovered, while 0 or below gives zero stun factor; some mapped Spine/Head calculations retain a 0.02 floor. Body-region usage multipliers are unitless strength scales: 1 leaves calculated pose-driving strength unchanged, 0.5 halves it, and 0 suppresses that region’s drive when applied. UpdateMuscleStates combines these values with the usage multipliers to set pose-driving strength. This is an active ragdoll: a body simulated by physics that tries to follow an intended pose.

Mods can read and change these values, but direct field writes do not run damage events or physical death/resurrection. Kill and Resurrect only reset this helper's data; the damage routines separately request PuppetMaster death when overall health is depleted. BaseEnemyConfig.ApplyTo can overwrite the live configuration fields.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.PuppetMasta.Weight
member.summary: A PuppetMaster setting that supplies either a stored float in mode or a value sampled from a curve in mode.

remarks.para: This setting has two modes: Float (0) uses floatValue, while Curve (1) evaluates its Unity AnimationCurve. A curve maps an input to a float. In Curve mode, GetValue passes its param argument directly as that input; this type defines no unit or fixed interpretation for it.

For example, with Float mode and floatValue set to 0.5, GetValue(2) returns 0.5. With Curve mode and a curve assigned, GetValue(2) returns the curve's output at input 2. Curve mode requires a non-null curve; the native method enters a non-returning failure path if the curve is missing. The meaning and units of the returned float depend on the PuppetMaster setting that uses this object.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.PuppetMasta.Weight.Mode
member.summary: Chooses how gets a float: returns the stored value, while samples the assigned curve.

remarks.para: An enum is a named set of integer choices. Here Float (0) and Curve (1) are mode codes, not the resulting weight value. In Float mode, Weight.GetValue returns Weight.floatValue and ignores its input parameter. In Curve mode, it passes that parameter directly to the assigned Unity AnimationCurve, which maps an input to a float.

For example, Float mode with floatValue set to 0.5 makes Weight.GetValue(2) return 0.5. With Curve mode and a curve assigned, Weight.GetValue(2) returns the curve's output at input 2. Curve mode requires a non-null curve; without one, the native method enters a non-returning failure path. This enum defines no unit or fixed meaning for the curve input or returned float; the setting that uses the Weight object supplies that meaning.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Marrow.RealHeptaAvatar
member.summary: RealHeptaAvatar is a Unity component that supplies proportions and local anchors for a tracked VR body. scales reference measurements to the player’s standing eye height, and computes derived dimensions.

remarks.para: Avatar is the Unity component that holds a character’s skeleton and body measurements. RealHeptaAvatar keeps reference distances in meters, unitless proportions, and stored local-position vectors in avatar/Animator-root-aligned axes. The Animator root is the transform anchoring the avatar skeleton; these vectors use axes aligned to it, not world positions or coordinates relative to an arbitrary child transform.
